title: `reads:` scopes and a world-hash in step identity
problem: Step identity is sha256(canonicalJson{kind, payload, schema, key}) (canonical.ts:35-37, runtime.ts:475). The working tree an agent greps is not in it — README deviation #5 says so outright. Two consequences: (a) a resume after the repo changed happily serves a journaled answer that was computed against a different tree, and verifyServe only covers a handful of git ops; (b) weft can never say *which* steps a repo change invalidated, which is why there is no cross-run reuse. `WriteScope` exists (sdk/types.ts:30-34) and has no read counterpart at all.
proposal: Add `reads?: ReadScope` alongside `write`. Before dispatch, ctx.ts computes a `worldHash` over the read scope: run `git ls-files -s -z` plus `ls-files --others --exclude-standard -z` against `integrationBaseCommit(cwd)` (ctx.ts:190-244 already produces that tree), filter paths through the existing `scopeMatcher` from @techery/weft-isolation, and sha256 the sorted `(path, mode, blobOid)` triples — blob oids come free from the index, so no file is read. Feed worldHash into `hashStep` as a fifth component and journal it on `step.scheduled`. A step with no `reads` keeps today's exact behaviour (worldHash undefined, hash unchanged — fully backward compatible with existing journals). Secondary win: the Claude tool gate can reuse the same matcher to deny out-of-scope *reads*, closing the asymmetry where scope only constrains writes.
priorArt: Burr declares `reads=[...]`/`writes=[...]` per action and validates them statically at graph-build time. Bazel and Nix hash declared inputs to decide what may be reused. No durable-execution engine (Temporal, Restate, DBOS, Inngest, Vercel WDK) models the filesystem as part of step identity at all — this is genuinely open ground for a repo-aware engine.
risks: Over-broad scopes (`src/**`) make worldHash change on every commit, so salvage stops working exactly where it is most valuable — needs a `weft explain --why-rerun` to make invalidation legible. Untracked-file enumeration on huge repos costs a `ls-files` per step; cache it per integration-base sha inside the runtime. Read scopes are also a lie for agents that shell out (`rg` outside the scope), so `mode:"strict"` is only honest on providers with a live tool hook — Codex has none.
fitsArchitecture: sdk (ReadScope type), core/canonical (hashStep arity), core/ctx (compute + pass), core/events (step.scheduled gains worldHash), core/replay (match on the extended hash — no change needed, it is already opaque), isolation (export a `treeDigest(cwd, scope)` next to scopeMatcher), provider-claude/gate.ts (read denial). Additive: journals without worldHash keep matching.

title: Cross-run step cache keyed on {identity, worldHash}
problem: Salvage only works *within* one run's journal (replay.ts:248-301). Running the same review workflow over 20 PRs, or re-running it on an unchanged repo after a failure, re-pays for every read-only analysis step. The engine already content-addresses steps and already stores outputs in a sha256 blob store — the only missing piece is a lookup that spans runs. Meanwhile blobs accumulate forever with no GC (stores.ts:88-93), so weft is paying the storage cost of a cache without having one.
proposal: Add a `CacheStore` alongside JournalStore/BlobStore: `get(cacheKey)` / `put(cacheKey, entry)` where cacheKey = sha256(hash) and hash already folds in worldHash from idea #1. Opt in per step with `cache: { ttl?: Duration; scope?: "repo" | "none" }`, defaulting to off for anything with a `write` scope or a side effect (only agent/check/fetch/sideeffect kinds are eligible; git writes never are). On a cache hit runtime.runStep journals a new `cache.hit { seq, cacheKey, fromRunId }` event plus a normal `step.completed` carrying the cached output and `usage: { input:0, output:0, usd:0, cached:true }`, so the run's report can show "14 steps served from cache, $3.40 avoided". FsCacheStore is a directory of JSON pointers into the existing blob store, so `weft prune` can mark-and-sweep blobs reachable from live journals *and* live cache entries.
priorArt: LangGraph's node-level `CachePolicy(cache_key, ttl)`; Hatchet's `ctx.memo` as a lighter tier than a full checkpoint; Helicone's response cache at the gateway (claimed up to 95% cost reduction on cacheable traffic); Bazel's action cache is the canonical shape (declared inputs → content-addressed outputs).
risks: A cache hit on a step whose real inputs are wider than its declared `reads` silently serves a stale answer — this is why cache must be opt-in and why `reads` should be *required* to enable it. Cross-run reuse also crosses budget boundaries: a cached step charges nothing, which is correct but makes budget projections non-reproducible between a cold and warm run. Needs a prominent `--no-cache` and a cache-hit line in `weft report`.
fitsArchitecture: core/stores (CacheStore interface + MemoryCacheStore), store-fs (FsCacheStore + sweep), core/runtime (lookup between the replay match and the live dispatch — one new branch in runStep), core/events (cache.hit), sdk (CacheOptions on AgentOptions/CheckOptions), host/weft.ts (wire the store), cli (`weft cache`), projections (report line). Depends on idea #1 for correctness.

title: Record-and-replay the nondeterministic globals instead of banning them
problem: The gate bans `Date.now`, `new Date()`, `Math.random`, timers, `Intl`, and locale methods across eleven AST rules (gate/rules.ts:57-72) and the node:vm sandbox makes them throw. The replacements are `ctx.now()`, `ctx.random()`, `ctx.uuid()` — all async and all costing a journal record each. So a workflow that wants a formatted timestamp in a prompt must `await ctx.now()`, and a helper library that innocently calls `Date.now()` in a log line fails `weft check` with no recourse. This is the single largest authoring tax weft charges, and it buys a guarantee that other engines get for free by recording rather than prohibiting.
proposal: Make the sandboxed globals replay-stable rather than absent. (1) `Date.now()` / `new Date()` return the runtime's *logical clock*: the `at` of the most recent journaled record for this run — which already exists on every JournalRecord, so this needs zero new events and is monotonic by construction. (2) `Math.random()` is a seeded PRNG (xoshiro128**) whose 128-bit seed is journaled once in `run.created`; the sandbox re-seeds and fast-forwards by the recorded draw count, which is journaled on `step.scheduled` as `entropy: n` so mid-run divergence is detectable. (3) `crypto.randomUUID` derives from the same PRNG. (4) Demote `no-date-now`, `no-argless-date`, `no-math-random` from errors to off-by-default informational rules; keep `no-timers`, `no-global-fetch`, `no-process-env`, `no-bare-import` as hard errors, since those are effects, not entropy. `ctx.now()`/`ctx.random()` stay for callers who want an explicit journaled record.
priorArt: Temporal's TS SDK replaces Math.random with a seeded PRNG and pins Date.now to the last Workflow Task completion time; Vercel Workflow DevKit documents that "Math.random and Date constructors are fixed in workflow runs… the framework ensures the values don't change across replays"; Golem records every WASI host-function result (clocks, randomness, I/O) in its oplog and replays it. weft is currently the only project in this space that bans rather than records.
risks: The logical clock is coarse — it only advances when something is journaled — so a tight loop measuring elapsed time sees zero, which is arguably correct but surprising. The entropy cursor must be journaled per step or an edit that changes draw counts silently shifts every later draw; make cursor drift a `replay.diverged` reason. Demoting rules is a semver-visible behaviour change for `weft check`, so it wants a config flag (`gate.entropy: "record" | "ban"`) with `ban` staying available.
fitsArchitecture: gate/load.ts (sandbox globals), gate/rules.ts (rule severity table + config), core/runtime (logicalNow(), prng, entropy cursor on step.scheduled), core/events (run.created.seed), core/engine (seed generation + restore on resume), host/config.ts (gate.entropy). The vm seam already exists — this replaces throwers with implementations behind it.

title: `weft fork <run> --from <step>` — the journal as an exploration surface
problem: The journal holds every input, output, and decision, and the only verbs over it are `resume`, `cancel`, and `replay --dry`. There is no way to say "the plan step at seq 4 was wrong, here is the right answer, re-run everything after it" — the operator's only option is to edit the workflow and hope salvage lands the way they want, or start over and re-pay for the whole prefix. This is recovery-only durability; every mature engine in the field has a fork verb.
proposal: `Engine.fork(runId, { fromIndex | fromStep, set?, newRunId? })`: copy journal records `[0, cut)` into a fresh run id, append `run.forked { parentRunId, fromIndex }` as the first new record, then optionally append synthetic `step.completed` records for `--set key=<json>` overrides (validated against the journaled `schemaJson` before they land, reusing the same structuralCheck path answers go through). Re-pin any `refs/weft/snapshots/*` the copied prefix references so a `git gc` between fork and resume cannot orphan them, and carry the parent's blob refs by reference (blobs are content-addressed and immutable, so no copying). The forked run resumes normally — the existing replay machinery does the rest, and the truncated suffix simply isn't there to match against.
priorArt: DBOS `forkWorkflow(workflowID, startStep, { newWorkflowID, applicationVersion, replacementChildren })`, plus bulk fork from the Conductor UI for fleet recovery after a bad deploy. LangGraph `update_state()` writes a new checkpoint on the parent and invoking with a `checkpoint_id` forks an alternate timeline (Studio exposes rewind/edit/re-run). Burr forks from an explicit `(app_id, partition_key, sequence_id)` triple. CrewAI Flows distinguishes `restore_from_state_id` (fork, fresh id) from `kickoff(inputs={'id'})` (resume, same lineage).
risks: A fork whose prefix contains a `patch.merged` inherits a working tree the new run did not produce — the fork must either refuse when the cut point is after an integrate, or checkout the journaled `resultTree` first. Overridden outputs bypass the provider entirely, so `--set` is a foot-gun for anyone who forgets the downstream steps were never re-validated against it; validating against the journaled schema at fork time is the mitigation. Child runs referenced by `step.scheduled.childRunId` in the carried prefix need the DBOS `replacementChildren` treatment or they will be re-entered.
fitsArchitecture: core/engine (fork()), core/events (run.forked), store-fs (bulk record copy + snapshot re-pin), cli/commands/fork.ts, daemon/app.ts (POST route + a Fork button next to Resume/Cancel), mcp/tools.ts (weft_fork), index-sqlite (parent lineage column). Reuses the existing appendIf, blob store, and replay paths unchanged.

title: Checkpoint records, journal compaction, and blob GC
problem: `ReplayIndex.fromRecords` folds the entire journal from record 0 on every resume, every `weft status`, every daemon read, and every projection refresh (replay.ts:90-238, store-fs/journal.ts:467-520). A long-lived run — a week-long review loop with 3,000 steps and repeated resumes — pays that fold repeatedly, and `list()` folds every run's journal. Separately there is no blob GC at all: transcripts, patches, and every >64KB step output accumulate under `.weft/blobs` forever with no prune verb.
proposal: Add a `checkpoint` event that embeds a serialized ReplayIndex digest: completions keyed by hash/key with blob-ref outputs (never inline values), `totalUsage`, `maxSeq`, `maxHumanId`, `mergedBaseTrees`, and the standing human answers. The engine appends one every N records (default 500) and at every quiescence point (before a durable wait). `ReplayIndex.fromRecords` gains a fast path: scan backwards for the newest `checkpoint`, hydrate from it, then fold only records after it. Because a checkpoint is a pure fold of what precedes it, it is *advisory* — a corrupt or unparseable checkpoint is skipped and the full fold runs, so this can never make a run unresumable. Then `weft prune` does mark-and-sweep blob GC: walk every journal (plus cache entries from idea #2), collect `$blob` refs, delete the rest; `weft prune --runs --older-than 90d --status complete` compacts finished runs to `run.created` + last checkpoint + terminal.
priorArt: Temporal's Event History has hard size/count limits and forces `continueAsNew` to bound it. Microsoft Agent Framework writes an entry checkpoint before the first superstep and again when external responses are delivered, explicitly so "the complete workflow run is replayable". Golem exposes configurable persistence levels and atomic regions to trade oplog volume against recovery granularity. Trigger.dev, Langfuse, and Temporal all have retention policies; weft has none.
risks: A checkpoint that disagrees with the records it claims to cover is worse than none — hence advisory-only and a `weft doctor --verify-checkpoints` that re-folds and compares. Compacting completed runs destroys forensic detail the report may not capture; gate it behind an explicit flag and never compact a run that is not terminal. Blob GC racing a live run appending a new blob needs the sweep to take the same cross-process lock the appender uses, or to only sweep blobs older than the oldest live claim.
fitsArchitecture: core/events (checkpoint), core/replay (hydrate/apply split — `fromRecords` currently has one big switch that becomes `apply(rec)`), core/engine (emit cadence + quiescence hook), core/stores (BlobStore gains `list()`/`delete()`), store-fs (implement both + prune), cli/commands/prune.ts, cli doctor. Nothing outside core needs to know checkpoints exist.

title: Multi-worker execution: the journal as a work queue
problem: A run is single-process by construction: `acquireRun` claims it, one RunRuntime executes every step, and the global limiter caps concurrency at `min(16, cpus-2)` on that one machine (config.ts:66-68, engine.ts:249-256). A 200-way `ctx.parallel` fan-out of worktree write steps is bounded by one laptop's cores and disk. Yet every primitive needed to distribute already exists: `appendIf` for CAS, `acquireRun` leases with TTL and fencing, and an external-event tailer that already converts foreign appends (human.answered, signal.received, run.cancelled) into in-process deliveries (engine.ts:908-951).
proposal: Add a `step.offered { seq, hash, kind, payload, worldHash, leaseTtlMs }` event and a `StepClaim` store method (CAS on `.weft/claims/<runId>/<seq>.json`, same protocol as `acquireRun`). A step marked `distributable` (agent steps with `isolation:"worktree"` and a declared `reads`/`write` scope — i.e. steps whose whole world is declared) is offered rather than executed: the owner journals `step.offered`, marks the step waiting (the existing `markWaiting`/suspension machinery), and parks. A `weft worker --repo <url|path>` process polls for offers, claims one, clones/fetches to the declared base commit, executes the step against its own provider credentials and its own budget slice, and appends `step.completed` through `appendIf`. The owner's tailer picks the completion up exactly as it picks up a human answer today — no new delivery path. Budget stays correct because the worker appends real `usage` and the owner's `charge()` runs on the tailer delivery.
priorArt: Windmill: stateless API servers advance flow state in Postgres while stateless workers pull individual job rows, with dead workers detected via `worker_ping` heartbeats and a reaper marking their jobs failed. Temporal task queues and worker fleets. Hatchet and Inngest both pull steps from a durable queue. Trigger.dev deploys each task as a container image. weft would be the first to do it with the journal *itself* as the queue and no server.
risks: This is the idea that can compromise every other guarantee. A worker that dies mid-step leaves a claimed-but-incomplete step — the TTL reaper must journal `step.offered` again and the retry must be idempotent, which is exactly what `verifyServe` and per-attempt worktrees are for. Patch capture on a worker produces a diff against a base commit the owner must also have, so the base sha has to be pushed/fetchable — trivial for a shared remote, hard for a laptop. Budget admission (`reserveCall`) is per-process, so N workers each admit against their own view of headroom and the ceiling overshoots by up to N calls; the fix is a journaled reservation event, which adds an append to the hot path. Only offer steps whose read and write scopes are both declared, or the world-hash contract breaks.
fitsArchitecture: core/stores (claimStep + StepLease), store-fs (claim directory, same lock protocol as owner.lock), core/events (step.offered, step.claimed), core/runtime (a `distributable` branch in runStep that offers-and-waits instead of executing), core/engine (tailer already handles foreign appends; extend the switch), a new `packages/worker` or `weft worker` in cli, isolation (fetch-to-base rather than local worktree seed). Deliberately reuses the lease, fencing, appendIf, and suspension machinery already built for humans.

title: Retry policies as declared objects, with resumable backoff
problem: `retry` is `{ attempts, backoffMs? }` and the delay scales linearly (runtime.ts:726-751). The non-retryable set is hardcoded (`cancelled`, `budget_exceeded`, `gate_denied`, `human_denied`) — a workflow cannot say "retry a `fetch_failed` five times with exponential backoff and jitter, but never retry `invalid_output`". Worse, a run that crashes mid-backoff re-arms the *full* delay on resume, because the backoff sleep is not a `reuseIncomplete` step the way `ctx.sleep` and `ctx.signal` are. And `human_denied` is declared in the retry predicate and never thrown anywhere (a dead code path the inventory already flags).
proposal: Widen `RetryOptions` to `{ attempts, backoff?: "linear" | "exponential", base?: Duration, max?: Duration, jitter?: "none" | "full", on?: StepErrorCode[] | ((e: StepError) => boolean) }` with a workflow-level default in `meta.defaults.retry` and an engine-level default in config. Journal the decision, not just the fact: `step.attempt` gains `{ nextDelayMs, retryReason }`, and the backoff wait itself becomes a nested journaled sleep anchored to the failed attempt's timestamp — so a resume during a 10-minute backoff waits the remainder, exactly like `ctx.sleep`. The `on` predicate is only consulted for codes not in the hardcoded never-retry set, so cancellation and budget exhaustion stay non-negotiable.
priorArt: Temporal's RetryPolicy with initialInterval / backoffCoefficient / maximumInterval / nonRetryableErrorTypes. Cloudflare Workflows' declarative `retries: { limit, delay, backoff: 'exponential' }`. Hatchet and Inngest both expose per-step retry configuration with backoff. PocketFlow pairs `Node(max_retries, wait)` with an `exec_fallback` hook that returns a degraded result instead of propagating.
risks: A function predicate in `on` is workflow code running in the determinism sandbox on an error path — it must be treated as untrusted and its throw swallowed into "do not retry". Full jitter makes the delay nondeterministic, so it must draw from the journaled PRNG (idea #3) or be journaled in `step.attempt.nextDelayMs` and re-read on replay — the sketch does the latter, which works today. Exponential backoff with a 5m cap plus a step timeout can exceed a human's patience with no signal; surface remaining backoff in `weft status`.
fitsArchitecture: sdk/types.ts (RetryOptions, meta.defaults.retry), core/config.ts (limits.retry default), core/runtime.ts (the attempt loop at 726-751 — the delay computation and the `reuseIncomplete` anchor), core/events.ts (step.attempt fields), projections (show retry reason in the tree). Also the natural place to finally throw `human_denied` or delete it.

title: `ctx.await({ any: [...] })` — composable durable wait conditions
problem: weft has three durable waits — `ctx.signal(name, schema, {timeout})`, `ctx.sleep(d)`, and human steps with deadlines — and no way to compose them. "Wait for the CI signal, or a human override, or 24 hours, whichever comes first" has no expression. `Promise.race` over ctx steps is the obvious attempt and it is silently wrong: the losing arms stay journaled as incomplete scheduled entries, and on resume `reuseIncomplete` re-adopts them and re-arms their waits. The gate has no rule against it either — the docs/reviews file flags `Promise.race` as unfenced.
proposal: One journaled step with N arms. `ctx.await({ any: [...] })` (and `all`) takes wait *descriptors*, not promises: `ctx.wait.signal(name, schema)`, `ctx.wait.human(req)`, `ctx.wait.timer(duration)`. The step hashes over the ordered arm descriptors, uses `reuseIncomplete` so a resumed race keeps its original deadline anchor, and on resolution journals `wait.resolved { seq, arm, index }` before the completion. Replay reads the recorded arm index and returns that arm's value without re-arming anything — the race outcome is a journaled fact, not a re-run. Add a `no-promise-race` gate rule pointing at `ctx.await` as the fix-it, since that is now a real answer rather than a scold.
priorArt: Hatchet's `ctx.waitFor(Or(UserEventCondition(...), SleepCondition('24h')))` composes event waits and timeouts into one durable primitive; arrays mean AND, `Or(...)` means first-of. Temporal's `condition(predicate)` plus durable timers gets there with more ceremony. Inngest's `step.waitForEvent(id, { event, timeout, match })` composes exactly one event with one timeout. VoltAgent ships `andRace` as a first-class combinator.
risks: A human arm that loses the race has a pending `human.requested` in the journal that must be explicitly retired (a `human.withdrawn` event), or `weft status` shows a request nobody should answer and the daemon will happily accept an answer for it. Cross-process delivery races: the tailer could deliver a signal at the same moment the timer fires, so arm selection must go through `appendIf` the way answer delivery does. `all` combined with a timer is genuinely ambiguous (partial results?) — ship `any` first.
fitsArchitecture: sdk/types.ts (WaitDescriptor union, ctx.wait, ctx.await), core/runtime.ts (a multi-arm variant of the existing `takeOrAwaitSignal` + human wait, sharing the deadline-chunking helper), core/events.ts (wait.resolved, human.withdrawn), core/replay.ts (arm index lookup), gate/rules.ts (no-promise-race), projections (render the winning arm in the tree).

title: Speculative fan-out with preemption and automatic patch lifecycle
problem: `ctx.parallel` runs different work; there is no primitive for running the *same* work k ways and keeping the best. Doing it by hand today is a trap: k write steps produce k patches, and a run that ends with un-integrated, un-discarded patches fails with `unintegrated_patches` (engine.ts:824-831), so the author must remember to discard k-1 of them. There is also no way to stop the losers — an unpicked lane keeps burning budget until it finishes, because the only cancellation is run-wide. stdlib's `judgePanel` picks a winner among *attempts* but is pure orchestration over `ctx.agent` and knows nothing about patches, preemption, or budget sub-pools.
proposal: `ctx.speculate(k, fn, { pick, budget })`: run k lanes of a caller-supplied function, each with its own child budget slice (reusing `Budget` fraction-of-remaining, which already parent-links), each in its own worktree. As soon as `pick` (a predicate, or `"first"`, or a judge step) selects a winner, the engine aborts the losing lanes and journals `speculation.decided { seq, winner, preempted: [...] }` plus a `step.preempted` per aborted lane. Any `PatchRef` produced by a loser is auto-discarded (a `patch.discarded` per patch) so `unintegrated_patches` cannot fire, and the winner's patch flows into `ctx.integrate` normally. On replay the recorded winner index is authoritative — losers are not re-run, and their journaled spend is restored so the budget arithmetic stays honest.
priorArt: uzi launches dozens of agents on one task and lets a human pick — and its documented failure is exactly the missing evaluation step. Crystal/Nimbalyst is built around comparing multiple approaches to the same task. VoltAgent's `andRace`. weft's own stdlib `judgePanel` is the orchestration half; this is the engine half (preemption, patch lifecycle, budget slices) that judgePanel cannot reach.
risks: Preemption is best-effort — `withTimeout` already documents that an aborted attempt may keep running and mutating files, and here it is mutating a worktree whose patch was never captured. Per-attempt worktrees contain the damage but the zombie still burns provider tokens that the ceiling has already committed. k-way speculation multiplies spend by k for one result, so the budget slice must be enforced up front, not discovered afterwards. `pick` runs workflow code mid-fan-out and must itself be a journaled step or the decision is not reproducible.
fitsArchitecture: sdk/types.ts (ctx.speculate + SpeculateOptions), core/ctx.ts (lane construction reusing the parallel + worktree paths, plus the discard bookkeeping already in ctx.discard), core/budget.ts (child pools already support fraction-of-remaining), core/events.ts (speculation.decided, step.preempted), core/runtime.ts (per-lane AbortController), stdlib (rewrite judgePanel on top of it), projections (render preempted lanes).

title: Attempt checkpointing: keep the provider session across a timeout or crash
problem: When a step times out, `withTimeout` aborts the attempt, drains 5s to harvest late usage, and fails (runtime.ts:763-834). The retry starts a brand-new provider session from turn 0 — every token of the aborted attempt's context is thrown away and re-paid. The adapters already capture `sessionId` (Claude absorbs it from any SDK message; Codex copies `thread.id`) and already know how to resume a session, because that is exactly how `provider.repair` works. The information is in hand and gets discarded.
proposal: Two small changes. (1) On abort or timeout, journal the attempt's `sessionId` and partial transcript on the `step.attempt` record — the drain window already exists to harvest usage, so harvest the session id in the same place. (2) `StepIO` gains `priorSessionId`, and the agent execute path passes it to `provider.run` as a resume handle when present, prompting "you were interrupted; continue and produce the structured output" — which is nearly the finalize turn Claude's adapter already implements. Add `RunControl.checkpoint(partial)` to the provider seam so a long-running adapter can voluntarily journal progress before an abort lands. A resume after a *process crash* gets the same benefit: the incomplete `step.scheduled` is already re-adopted via `reuseIncomplete`, so the session id rides along with it.
priorArt: E2B pauses a sandbox with a full memory snapshot (~1s resume) so a long agent session is frozen rather than restarted. Claude Code's session transcripts persist under `~/.claude/projects/**` and `/resume` rehydrates from them. Golem's idempotence mode makes "on interruption, retry the external call or fail" an explicit per-call policy rather than a hidden default. Both weft adapters already resume sessions for schema repair — this is that mechanism pointed at a different trigger.
risks: Resuming a session whose abort was caused by the agent looping means resuming *into the loop* — the retry must carry a stricter instruction and a reduced `maxTurns`, and after one failed continuation it should fall back to a cold start. Session ids expire provider-side, so `resumeSessionId` must degrade to a fresh run rather than erroring. Whether the aborted turn's tokens were actually billed is provider-dependent, so the restored usage is a lower bound.
fitsArchitecture: core/provider.ts (AgentRequest.resumeSessionId, RunControl.checkpoint), core/runtime.ts (harvest in the existing drain window at 815-833; StepIO.priorSessionId alongside the existing priorScheduledAt), core/events.ts (step.attempt gains sessionId/transcriptRef), core/ctx.ts (pass through), provider-claude (map to Options.resume — already used for repair/finalize), provider-codex (map to resumeThread — already used for repair).

title: Incremental event index and `weft query`
problem: Nothing in core calls `indexRun` — the sqlite index is only ever rebuilt wholesale by the host (host/weft.ts:122-141), so rows are stale between rebuilds, and `search()` is an unranked LIKE scan with a default limit of 50. The index also stores one row per *run*, so per-step questions are unanswerable: which step keys burn the most tokens, how often the schema repair loop fires, which workflows diverge most on resume, what a given prompt cost across 40 runs. weft has the richest per-step record in this space and no way to ask it anything. Related: `budget.sampled` is appended best-effort (`void rt.append(...).catch(() => undefined)`), so the durable spend record is a lower bound by design.
proposal: Two parts. (1) An `IndexSink` seam on the engine that observes every appended record and upserts into a new `events` table (`run_id, i, at, type, seq, kind, key, label, phase, provider, model, tokens_in, tokens_out, usd, error_code, json`), written incrementally in the same tick as the append and idempotent on `(run_id, i)` so a rebuild and a live write converge. Make the spend record durable while you're there: replace best-effort `budget.sampled` with an awaited `usage.charged { seq, usage }` on the charge path — one append per model call, which also gives the index exact per-call cost attribution. (2) A typed query API plus a CLI verb over it, with `--json` output (which no weft command currently has).
priorArt: DBOS stores workflow status, inputs, and step outputs as ordinary relational rows you can query with SQL and join against your own tables — explicitly to enable ad-hoc analysis. Langfuse aggregates cost by user/session/tag/prompt-version. Opik derives metrics from traces with an analytics store (DuckDB local, ClickHouse prod). AgentOps normalizes cross-provider cost per session.
risks: Writing to sqlite on the append path adds latency and a second failure mode to the hot path — the sink must be strictly fire-and-forget with the journal remaining the only source of truth, and `weft doctor` must be able to rebuild from journals when the index drifts. Raw `--sql` is a support burden the moment the schema changes; version it with `PRAGMA user_version` (the index already does drift-detect-and-recreate) and treat the typed query API as the stable surface. An awaited `usage.charged` per model call roughly doubles journal record count for agent-heavy runs — pairs naturally with checkpointing (idea #5).
fitsArchitecture: index-sqlite (events table, schema v2, EventQuery), core/engine.ts (an optional `onAppend` sink, mirroring how the tailer already observes records), core/ctx.ts + budget.ts (usage.charged replacing best-effort budget.sampled), core/events.ts, host/weft.ts (wire the sink into the lazy sqlite index), cli/commands/query.ts (+ `--json` on ls/status/report/explain while you're in there), daemon (a query route).

title: `ctx.spawn` — non-blocking, durable sub-workflow handles
problem: `ctx.workflow` is a blocking call whose step deliberately never serves from the journal (`verifyServe: async () => false`, ctx.ts:1053-1059), so every resume re-enters the child run and relies on the child's own journal to avoid re-paying. That is correct but it forces a shape: the parent holds a live process for the entire duration of every child, and N children means N concurrent in-process re-entries. There is no way to launch a child, suspend the parent entirely, and collect the result later — which is exactly what you want for a fan-out of ten sub-workflows that each take an hour, or for a child that should outlive the parent.
proposal: `ctx.spawn(def, input, opts): Promise<ChildHandle<Out>>` starts the child run, journals its `childRunId` on `step.scheduled` (the field already exists), and returns immediately. `ctx.join(handle)` / `ctx.joinAll(handles)` is a durable wait: if the child is terminal, fold its journal for the output; if not, mark the parent waiting and let the parent's tailer deliver on the child's terminal event. Add `detached: true` for a child the parent does not join (fire-and-forget, still budget-linked). Because the child run id is journaled at spawn time, a resumed parent re-adopts the *same* child rather than launching a second one — the existing `reuseIncomplete` + childRunId reallocation logic (engine.ts:1088-1105) already handles the identity half. `ctx.workflow` becomes `spawn` + `join` and keeps its current semantics exactly.
priorArt: Temporal splits `startChild` (handle) from `executeChild` (blocking), and Nexus for cross-namespace calls. DBOS `startWorkflow` returns handles for background execution. Hatchet supports runtime-dynamic child spawning so the DAG is built as the agent decides, with the parent staying durable. Inngest's `step.invoke` awaits a typed result from another function.
risks: A parent that suspends while children run needs someone to actually drive those children — either each child holds its own process (which is what happens today, just without the parent parked) or this must land alongside the park/wake scheduler (idea #14) to be worth much. `detached` children break the budget roll-up invariant that a parent's spend covers its subtree, and break `unintegrated_patches` reasoning if the child produces patches. Cancelling a parent must decide the fate of detached children — cascade by default, with an opt-out.
fitsArchitecture: sdk/types.ts (ctx.spawn/join/joinAll, ChildHandle, SubWorkflowOptions.detached), core/ctx.ts (split the current ctx.workflow into spawn + join), core/engine.ts (`executeChildRun` already allocates and collision-checks child ids; add a non-blocking launch path and a terminal-event subscription), core/runtime.ts (join is a durable wait reusing markWaiting/suspensionOf, which already folds live children), core/events.ts (child.terminal delivery), projections (renderTree already nests by parentSeq — extend to child runs).

title: Make `replay --dry` faithful, then make it a CI gate
problem: `replayDry` is the tool for "what would happen if I resume this edited script" and it does not model that case: it never computes `positionsTrusted`, ignores `opts.defHash`, and constructs `new Budget({})` with `agentCounter: { count: 0 }` (engine.ts:1792-1827). So it under-reports divergence precisely for edited scripts — the ambiguous-keyless re-run path is invisible to it — and its cost estimate ignores both the restored spend and the budget ceiling that would actually stop the resume. Separately there is no regression test for replay behaviour at all: the docs/reviews file lists "no corpus replay gate" as an open finding, and a change to `matchStep` or `OrderedDelivery` could silently alter how every existing journal replays.
proposal: Two steps, both small. (1) Make `replayDry` share `resumeSetup`'s configuration: same `versionUnchanged` computation, same `defHash` plumbing, same budget restore (`max(journaled sum, last sample)` plus the descendant walk), same agent-counter restore. Report the ceiling verdict too — "would exceed the $5 ceiling at step 31". (2) Export `replayConformance(journalPath, def)` from @techery/weft-testing and add `weft conformance`: pin a run's journal as a golden file, then re-run `replayDry` over every golden in CI and fail when the `{hits, salvaged, diverged[]}` shape changes. That turns edit-tolerant replay from a claimed property into a tested one, using machinery that already exists.
priorArt: Temporal's `Worker.runReplayHistory()` / `runReplayHistories()` feeds recorded production histories through new code and throws `DeterminismViolationError` on divergence — the reference CI gate for replay safety. Google ADK's `adk conformance` records a scenario into golden YAML then defaults to Replay Mode, failing the command on any deviation, explicitly designed to block a PR. Resonate ships a public deterministic-simulation harness for its own SDK.
risks: Golden journals embed absolute cwds, run ids, timestamps, and blob refs — the baseline must compare the normalized `{hits, salvaged, diverged[]}` shape (the `journal.toJSON()` treatment testing already applies), not raw records. Blob-backed outputs in a golden need either inlining under the 64KB threshold or a committed fixture blob directory. And a faithful `replayDry` will report *more* divergence than today, which will look like a regression when it is the bug being fixed — worth calling out in the changelog.
fitsArchitecture: core/engine.ts (replayDry shares resumeSetup's config — mostly deletion of the divergent construction at 1792-1827), testing/src/conformance.ts (a third suite alongside journalStoreConformance and blobStoreConformance, same vitest-optional-peer pattern), cli/commands/conformance.ts, .github/workflows/ci.yml (add to the smoke job next to the existing `weft check`).

title: Park and wake: suspend a waiting run to zero
problem: A run blocked on a human holds a Node process, a worktree, and an ownership lease. Cancel and shutdown deliberately do *not* release the lease (engine.ts:1623-1631, 1696-1701) so the run stays claimed until TTL expiry, and there is no mechanism to persist-and-exit at a durable wait. A team with thirty pending code reviews holds thirty processes for days. Meanwhile `.weft` already contains everything needed to restart any of them from scratch, and the engine already knows when a run is suspended (`inflightLive === 0 && pending waits`, runtime.ts:418-446).
proposal: `Engine.park(runId)`: at a quiescence point with only durable waits outstanding, journal `run.parked { wakeAt?, pending: [...] }` (wakeAt = the earliest armed deadline across timers, human timeouts, and signal timeouts), write a checkpoint (idea #5), release the lease cleanly, tear down worktrees for attempts that are not in flight, and exit. A due-index at `.weft/parked/<wakeAt>-<runId>` gives O(1) "what is due" without folding journals. `weft wake` (one-shot, cron-friendly) and the daemon's scheduler loop both scan it: resume any parked run whose `wakeAt` has passed, or whose pending request just got answered — the daemon already has a wake-suspended-runs job for answers, this generalizes it to timers. Make parking the default for `--watch`-less CLI runs that hit a durable wait, so `weft run` returns the terminal instead of blocking on a human.
priorArt: Prefect distinguishes `pause_flow_run` (blocks in place) from `suspend_flow_run` (exits the process entirely, reschedules on resume) — two primitives for two wait durations. Restate handlers suspend rather than block, holding zero compute on a FaaS runtime. Golem workers suspend to zero memory and are resurrected by oplog replay. Cloudflare Durable Objects hibernate while keeping WebSockets alive. Vercel WDK's `sleep()` and `createWebhook()` free the process entirely.
risks: Parking must be refused while any live step is in flight, and a step that is only *nearly* done gets its work thrown away — so park at journaled boundaries only, and never mid-attempt. Worktrees for a parked run must survive (they hold uncaptured work) or be provably empty, which means teardown is only safe for attempts with a captured patch. Waking is only as reliable as whoever runs `weft wake`, so a parked run with no scheduler is a run that never finishes — the CLI must say so loudly, and the daemon should be the recommended host. Cleanly releasing the lease at park time is the right behaviour and reverses a deliberate current choice; the safety argument (no zombie can be writing at a journaled quiescence point) has to actually hold.
fitsArchitecture: core/engine.ts (park/wakeDue, plus the existing suspension detection at 768-785 as the trigger), core/events.ts (run.parked / run.woke), core/runtime.ts (quiescence assertion, deadline aggregation across the armed timers it already chunks), store-fs (due-index directory + cleanup), core/ctx.ts (worktree teardown policy), cli (`weft wake`, park-by-default on suspension), daemon/server.ts (scheduler loop generalizing the existing wakeIfSuspended job), mcp (weft_wait already long-polls — it would poll a parked run identically).

title: Route policies with typed fallback chains
problem: Routing today is a three-way merge of step opts → workflow defaults → config.defaults, resolved inline in `agentImpl` (ctx.ts:269-277). It is per-call-site and static: there is no way to say "all `review:*` steps go to Opus, fall back to Codex on provider_error or timeout" without writing try/catch in workflow code — which would create a SECOND step with a different identity hash and break salvage. Worse, `runStep`'s retry loop (runtime.ts:596-761) re-dispatches the same route on every attempt, so a provider outage burns every retry.
proposal: Add a `RoutePolicy` layer resolved between step opts and workflow defaults, matched by picomatch glob over the step key (picomatch is already a dependency in isolation/gate). A policy declares a primary route plus an ordered `fallback` list with `when` codes. Critical identity design: the step payload records the DECLARED policy id and primary route only, so the content hash is stable regardless of who actually answered; the route that served the call is recorded on `step.attempt` (`routedTo`) and on `step.completed`. A fallback hop is journaled as an ordinary `step.attempt` with `detail: "fallback claude→codex (provider_error)"`, so accumulated usage already rides the existing error-carried-usage path in `runProviderWithRepair`. Fallback is refused for the same non-retryable codes the retry predicate already refuses (cancelled, budget_exceeded, gate_denied, human_denied) — a budget ceiling must never be routed around. `weft explain` gains a `route: claude/claude-opus-5 → codex (fallback)` line.
priorArt: BAML composes `client` blocks into strategy clients with `retry_policy`, `fallback` chains and round-robin, declared once rather than at each call site. Pydantic AI's `FallbackModel` is an ordered chain that fails over automatically on provider error. Helicone's gateway does latency- and cost-aware routing with automatic failover (P2C + PeakEWMA). None of them keeps a stable content-addressed step identity across the hop, which is the part weft has to get right.
risks: Two real hazards. (1) Identity: if the actual route leaked into the payload hash a fallback would make the step un-salvageable on the next resume — the design deliberately hashes only the declared policy, but that means a journaled result from Codex gets served to a step declared as Claude, which must be visible in `explain`/`report` or it is a silent surprise. (2) Cost asymmetry: falling back from a priced model to an unpriced one under a USD-only ceiling re-triggers the `reportsUsd` refusal mid-run, so fallback candidates must be pre-validated for pricing at schedule time, not at hop time.
fitsArchitecture: `sdk/src/types.ts` (RoutePolicy, AgentOptions.route), `core/src/config.ts` (routes field + resolver, alongside the existing approvalPolicy glob machinery), `core/src/ctx.ts` (route resolution in agentImpl, fallback loop around `runProviderWithRepair`), `core/src/events.ts` (`routedTo` on step.attempt, `policy` on step.scheduled), `host/src/config.ts` (Zod section, strict-inside like every other section), `cli/src/commands/explain.ts` + `core/src/projections.ts` (render the hop).

title: Native structured-output path with per-provider output-mode negotiation
problem: `ProviderCapabilities.structured` is declared as `"native" | "tool"` (provider.ts:65) but the Claude adapter hard-codes `structured: "tool"` and every single step pays an sdk-mcp round trip: a `weft` MCP server is spun up per stream, the model must call `mcp__weft__structured_output`, and the schema is restated in both the tool description and an appended `## Output` section. The README lists native JSON mode as unwired. Codex already does the native thing (`TurnOptions.outputSchema`), so weft pays a per-step tax on its primary provider that its secondary provider does not pay — and the budget ceilings make that tax visible in dollars.
proposal: Make the output channel an engine decision rather than an adapter constant. Add `outputMode` to `AgentRequest` and let the engine pick it from `capabilities().structured` plus a per-provider config override (`providers.claude.structuredMode: "native" | "tool" | "auto"`). In native mode the Claude adapter passes the already-object-rooted wire schema straight through the SDK's structured-output option, skips `createSdkMcpServer` entirely, and drops the tool-description restatement (keeping the shorter `## Output` note). When a native turn ends with nothing captured, the adapter degrades to the tool path within the same step and journals `step.attempt "native output empty → tool mode"` — so the fallback is auditable and its spend is charged through the existing accumulation path. `weft doctor` reports the negotiated mode per provider so the choice is never invisible.
priorArt: LangGraph's `create_agent` auto-selects `ProviderStrategy` (native constrained decoding on OpenAI/Anthropic/Gemini/xAI) versus `ToolStrategy` (schema as a tool call) per provider — exactly this negotiation. The Codex adapter inside weft already demonstrates the native path with `toStrictSchema` + `TurnOptions.outputSchema`. DSPy's Adapters make the output encoding a swappable strategy behind a stable typed contract.
risks: Native strict modes constrain generation and can suppress the free-form reasoning the tool path allows before the terminating call — a measurable quality regression risk on hard coding steps, and the reason the mode must be configurable rather than forced. Claude's native schema surface has its own strictness quirks (weft's Codex adapter already has to rewrite `required` and set `additionalProperties:false`); similar adaptation may be needed and must not mutate `const`/`enum`/`default` literals. Also the tool path's `capturedValue` boxing preserves a legitimate `null` answer; the native path must preserve that too.
fitsArchitecture: `core/src/provider.ts` (capabilities widening, `outputMode` on AgentRequest), `core/src/ctx.ts` (mode selection next to the existing USD-ceiling refusal), `core/src/config.ts` + `host/src/config.ts` (`structuredMode` under providers), `provider-claude/src/index.ts` (native branch; tool server extracted to a method), `provider-codex/src/index.ts` (report `structured: "native"` honestly), `cli/src/commands/doctor.ts`.

title: Schema-aligned coercion pass before spending a repair turn
problem: `runProviderWithRepair` (ctx.ts:813-882) goes straight from a failed `validateSchema` to `provider.repair(...)` — a full extra model turn, charged to the budget, up to `limits.repair` times, and on exhaustion the whole paid step dies with `schema_repair_exhausted`. But a large share of real failures are mechanical, not semantic: a ```json fence, prose before the object, a stringified number where the schema says number, a single value where an array is expected, a double-wrapped `{result:{value:…}}`. weft already owns a JSON-Schema keyword walker (`structuralCheck`, jsonschema.ts:86-213) that knows everything needed to fix these — it just uses it to reject rather than to repair.
proposal: Insert one pure, zero-model-call coercion pass between `unwrapWireValue` and the repair loop. `coerceToSchema(value, wireSchema)` attempts a bounded, schema-directed set of edits and returns `{ changed, value, applied }`; the engine only re-validates against the REAL Standard Schema, so coercion can never widen what is accepted — it can only turn a near-miss into a candidate the authoritative schema still has to approve. When coercion rescues a step, journal `step.attempt` with `detail: "coerced (no model call)"` and set `coerced: true` on `step.completed`, so `renderReport` can print a coercion rate and a team can see which prompts are drifting. Coercion never runs on a value that already validates.
priorArt: BAML's Schema-Aligned Parsing is exactly this: a schema-aware least-edit-distance coercion in Rust, claimed sub-10ms, fixing fences, trailing commas, unquoted keys, wrong-typed values, prose wrappers and partial objects. BAML's published Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard numbers show large first-pass gains from SAP alone (Claude 3 Haiku 57.3% → 91.7%, GPT-4o-mini 19.8% → 92.4%). Instructor and Pydantic AI both go straight to a retry and pay a model turn for it.
risks: Over-eager coercion is a correctness hazard, not just a quality one — `"scalar"` turning `"0"` into `0`, or `"wrap-array"` hiding that the model returned one item when it should have returned several. Mitigations: every fix is gated on an explicit schema keyword, the authoritative Zod schema still has the final say, and the applied fix list is journaled so a suspicious pattern is visible. `"extract"` on text containing multiple candidate objects must pick deterministically (first balanced value) or replay stops being reproducible.
fitsArchitecture: New `core/src/coerce.ts` beside `jsonschema.ts`, reusing its keyword walker; `core/src/ctx.ts` (one branch in `runProviderWithRepair`); `core/src/events.ts` (`coerced?: boolean` on step.completed); `core/src/projections.ts` (coercion count in the report ledger); table-driven cases in `testing/`. No new dependency, no gate rule change.

title: Per-step tool surface: MCP servers plus an allow/deny matrix
problem: `ToolPolicy` is `{ allowEdits: boolean; deny?: string[] }` (provider.ts:8-13) and that is the entire tool surface a weft step can express. Two consequences. First, a step cannot be GIVEN a tool it does not already have — no Linear MCP server for a triage step, no docs server for a review step — so weft workflows are strictly less capable than the same agent run under Claude Code. Second, the Claude gate's terminal clause is `return allow` (gate.ts:232): anything it does not specifically recognise — WebFetch, WebSearch, Task/subagent spawning, any other MCP server's tools — is unconditionally permitted even on a read-only step under a strict write scope.
proposal: Grow `ToolPolicy` into a declared, journaled, default-deny-capable matrix and add MCP server specs. `tools.allow` flips the gate's terminal clause from allow to deny for any tool not named (opt-in per step, so absent `allow` keeps today's behaviour). `tools.mcp` carries server specs whose `env` values may be `SecretHandle`s — resolved on the live path only via the existing `resolveSecretValues`, so the journal records `<redacted:LINEAR_KEY>` exactly as exec/bash env maps already do. The declared tool surface goes INTO the step payload and therefore the identity hash, because changing what a step may call is a semantic change to the step. Providers declare `toolPolicy: "enforced" | "advisory"` in capabilities and the engine refuses a `strict`-scoped step on an advisory provider rather than silently downgrading — the honest fix for the Claude/Codex asymmetry.
priorArt: opencode declares a permission matrix per agent — read/edit/bash/glob/grep/task each set to allow|ask|deny — far more expressive than a mode. goose's recipe `extensions` block is least-privilege by construction: naming extensions EXCLUDES the platform defaults. Claude Code and Codex CLI both let a subagent declare its MCP servers and denied tools in frontmatter/TOML. Windmill derives LLM tool JSON Schemas from typed script signatures so tool definitions cannot drift from implementations.
risks: Putting the tool surface in the identity hash means adding one MCP server invalidates every affected step on the next resume — correct, but it needs a loud `replay.diverged` reason so it does not read as a bug. MCP server lifecycle is the harder problem: a stdio server spawned per step multiplies process count across a 20-way fan-out and must be counted inside `globalLimiter`, not outside it. And a secret handed to a third-party MCP server leaves weft's redaction boundary the moment that server logs it — the journal stays clean but the blast radius does not.
fitsArchitecture: `core/src/provider.ts` (ToolPolicy, McpServerSpec, capabilities.toolPolicy), `sdk/src/types.ts` (`AgentOptions.tools`), `core/src/ctx.ts` (payload inclusion, secret resolution reusing the exec/bash path at ctx.ts:109-158, strict-on-advisory refusal beside the USD-ceiling refusal), `provider-claude/src/gate.ts` + `index.ts` (allow-list terminal clause, `mcpServers` merge alongside the existing weft server), `provider-codex/src/index.ts` (map to its MCP config; report `toolPolicy: "advisory"`), `host/src/config.ts` (workspace-level default servers).

title: Declared step capabilities backed by a real OS sandbox and a network allow-list
problem: weft's README is honest that `node:vm` is a determinism fence, not a security boundary — but that caveat is about the workflow body. The agent's own process has no boundary at all. A write step's worktree isolates files by convention: the process can `fs.writeFile` anywhere, open any socket, or install anything globally, and weft only learns about escapes from provider-self-reported `filesTouched` (posix-only detection, `isAbsolute(p) || p.startsWith("../")`, ctx.ts:631). Meanwhile `ctx.fetch` allows every host unless `fetchAllow` is configured, and that field is optional and undefined by default (config.ts:52-55), so the hardened per-hop redirect path is skipped entirely on a default install. The agent's network is not even nominally controlled.
proposal: Add a `sandbox` declaration per step and a pluggable `StepSandbox` seam behind it, mirroring how `TestHooks` and `AgentProvider` are already seams. A new `@techery/weft-sandbox` package ships three backends: `none` (today's behaviour, made explicit), `os` (bubblewrap on Linux, Seatbelt on macOS — writes allow-only scoped to the step's worktree, reads deny-then-allow), and an egress proxy enforcing a domain allow-list injected as `HTTPS_PROXY` into the agent's environment. The asymmetric defaults are the important part and are lifted from Anthropic's sandbox-runtime: reads permissive, writes allow-only, network deny-all-with-allowlist. Every denial is journaled as `sandbox.denied {seq, kind, target}` — making the sandbox a diagnostic surface, not just a fence. A two-phase form matters for real repos: `sandbox: { setup: { net: [...] }, run: { net: [] } }` lets a declared dependency-install phase have network and the agent phase have none.
priorArt: Anthropic's own sandbox-runtime (`srt`, Apache-2.0) does precisely this shape: bubblewrap on Linux, Seatbelt on macOS, a dedicated account with WFP egress filtering on Windows, plus a host proxy enforcing a domain allow-list — with reads deny-then-allow and writes allow-only as the documented default asymmetry. Codex CLI has `sandbox_mode` (read-only / workspace-write / danger-full-access) via Seatbelt/Landlock/seccomp with `.git` protected even in writable modes, and treats `approval_policy` as an ORTHOGONAL axis. GitHub Copilot's coding agent ships a network firewall on by default with a configurable allow-list. container-use gives each agent a container so installs and daemons are discarded with the step.
risks: Platform coverage is the whole difficulty: bubblewrap and Seatbelt are namespace/profile mechanisms, not virtualization, and CI runners without the right namespaces will not have them — so `backend: "auto"` must degrade LOUDLY (a journaled note plus a doctor warning), never silently. Over-tight write allow-lists break builds in confusing ways; the setup/run split mitigates but does not remove that. The egress proxy adds a TLS-interception decision weft should refuse to make: allow-list by SNI/CONNECT host only, never MITM. And a `sandbox` declaration belongs in the identity hash, which means adopting it invalidates existing journals once.
fitsArchitecture: New `packages/sandbox` (peer of `isolation`: pure functions plus a small seam), `sdk/src/types.ts` (`AgentOptions.sandbox`), `core/src/ctx.ts` (wrap the provider dispatch inside the existing `globalLimiter.with(...)` lane, just outside `providerLimiter`), `core/src/events.ts` (`sandbox.denied`), `core/src/config.ts` + `host/src/config.ts` (workspace defaults and a `sandbox.require: true` policy admins can set), `provider-codex/src/index.ts` (map to native `sandboxMode` rather than double-sandboxing), `cli/src/commands/doctor.ts` and `explain.ts`.

title: AgentProvider conformance suite
problem: The README's package table says the provider adapters sit "behind a shared conformance suite". There is none: `@techery/weft-testing/conformance` exports only `journalStoreConformance` and `blobStoreConformance` (conformance.ts:26, :137). The two adapters are verified by hand-written, mutually inconsistent test files (~40 cases for Claude, ~24 for Codex), and the divergences that matter most are exactly the ones nobody asserts — Codex silently ignores `maxTurns`, `onMaxTurns` and `tools.deny`, always returns `filesTouched: []`, and has no permission hook, while `ProviderHitl.onAsk` is declared, fenced against zombie attempts, and never called by any shipped adapter. `provider-mock` has no test directory at all.
proposal: Ship `agentProviderConformance(name, expected)` as a third `describe()` block in the conformance entry point, encoding exactly what the engine relies on: (1) `run()` returns output the declared wire schema accepts, or throws; (2) `repair()` re-prompts the same session when `sessionResume` is true and still returns a candidate when `sessionId` is undefined; (3) an already-aborted `ctl.signal` throws before any vendor call, and an abort mid-stream settles or throws without returning a stale result; (4) `usage` components are non-negative and `usd` is present iff `reportsUsd`; (5) capability HONESTY — if `permissionHook` is true a high-risk tool request must actually reach `hitl.onPermission`; if `toolPolicy` is `"enforced"` an out-of-scope edit must be refused before it lands; if it is `"advisory"` the suite asserts the adapter does not claim otherwise. The suite drives the adapter through a scripted fake vendor client, which both adapters already accept by injection (`queryFn` / lazy client).
priorArt: weft's own `journalStoreConformance` / `blobStoreConformance` are the template — same idea, one layer over. Resonate HQ runs Deterministic Simulation Testing against its server AND every SDK with the harnesses public, plus a differential tester comparing implementations against one workload. AutoGen's `ReplayChatCompletionClient` shows the right framing for the scripted side: a provider whose entire behaviour is "return the next scripted item", so the real routing, budget and journal paths are exercised with zero special-casing.
risks: Low and mostly self-inflicted: the suite will fail on day one for Codex, which is the point — but it turns a documentation inaccuracy into a red build, so the capability fields must be corrected in the same change or CI stays broken. Scripting a vendor SDK's message stream couples the suite to that SDK's message shape; keeping the fake behind a small `ScriptedTurn` type rather than the vendor's own types limits the blast radius when a vendor SDK changes.
fitsArchitecture: `testing/src/conformance.ts` (third exported suite; vitest stays an optional peer dependency exactly as today), no new export path needed (same `./conformance` subpath), new `provider-claude/test/conformance.test.ts` and `provider-codex/test/conformance.test.ts`, and the first test directory for `provider-mock`. `core/src/provider.ts` gains the honest capability fields the suite checks.

title: Prompt-prefix cache-aware fan-out scheduling
problem: A keyed `ctx.parallel` fan-out — the canonical weft shape, and what `.weft/workflows/review.ts` does — launches N agent steps sharing a long identical prefix (system framing, the write-scope paragraph appended at ctx.ts:485-493, the `## Output` schema section) that differ only in a short suffix. All N are released simultaneously by `globalLimiter` (default min(16, cpus−2)), so every one of them WRITES the shared prefix into the provider's cache and none of them reads it. `Usage.cacheRead` already exists and is populated by the Claude adapter, so weft can see the miss and does nothing about it. On a 20-file review this is a recurring overpayment against a budget ceiling weft enforces to the cent.
proposal: Add a prefix-cache scheduler in front of the provider limiter. Group in-flight agent dispatches by `(providerId, model, prefixHash)`, where `prefixHash` comes from an explicit `cachePrefix` a workflow or stdlib pattern declares (falling back to a hash of the prompt's leading bytes). The first member of a group dispatches immediately; siblings park until the leader's first usage report lands or `limits.prefixStaggerMs` (default 5000) elapses, whichever is sooner. This is pure scheduling: no journal event, no identity change, and it composes with `reserveCall` because parking happens BEFORE the budget reservation is taken, not after. Surface the payoff in `renderReport`'s cost line as `cached: N tokens (M%)` so the win is measured rather than asserted.
priorArt: Claude Code's dynamic workflows do exactly this and ship the knob: same-prefix agents are deliberately staggered up to `CLAUDE_CODE_WORKFLOW_PREFIX_STAGGER_MS` (default 5000ms) so siblings hit the first agent's prompt cache. It is the only cost optimisation of its kind in the surveyed landscape, and it lives in the harness weft dispatches to. Windmill's for-loop "squash onto one worker" locality option is the same instinct at a different layer.
risks: It trades latency for cost, and the trade is wrong for small fan-outs — a 2-way parallel of short steps pays up to 5s for a cache that saves little, so the scheduler should skip groups below a size threshold. If the leader fails fast without reporting usage, siblings must not wait the full stagger: `release()` has to fire on the failure path too, including the abandoned-attempt path that currently charges without journaling. And the grouping key is a heuristic — hashing the whole prompt makes every sibling its own group and the feature silently does nothing, which is why the explicit `cachePrefix` opt-in matters more than the automatic derivation.
fitsArchitecture: `core/src/limiter.ts` (PrefixScheduler beside the existing FIFO Semaphore), `core/src/ctx.ts` (wrap the provider call; release inside `chargeUsage` and on the failure/abandon paths), `core/src/config.ts` + `host/src/config.ts` (`limits.prefixStaggerMs`), `sdk/src/types.ts` (`AgentOptions.cachePrefix`), `stdlib/src/*.ts` (fan-out patterns declare their shared prefix), `core/src/projections.ts` (cacheRead in the cost line).

title: Session handoff: continue a prior step's provider session instead of re-reading the repo
problem: `DetailedAgentResult.sessionId` is returned by the engine and journaled on `step.completed`, both adapters implement session resume, and `capabilities().sessionResume` is true for Claude, Codex and mock — but nothing in the authoring surface can use it. The only consumer is the internal repair loop. So a two-stage workflow (`plan` then `implement`) pays for the implement step to re-discover everything the plan step already read: the same file reads, the same greps, the same context window rebuilt from zero. Under weft's own budget ceilings that is the single most expensive avoidable pattern in a multi-step coding workflow.
proposal: Add `continueFrom` to `AgentOptions`, taking a prior `DetailedAgentResult` (or a bare sessionId). When the target provider reports `sessionResume`, the engine passes `resume: prior.sessionId` into `AgentRequest` and the adapter continues that thread. Identity: the payload records `continuesFrom: <prior step's hash>` — the HASH, not the session id, because the session id is a vendor artefact that changes between runs while the logical dependency does not. Two degradations, both explicit and journaled: if the prior step routed to a different provider, or the vendor no longer holds the session (a resume days later), the engine falls back to `digest` mode — prepending the prior step's schema-validated value plus the head of its journaled transcript blob — and journals `step.attempt "session handoff unavailable → digest"`. That keeps the workflow correct across resumes without pretending the session survived.
priorArt: Aider's architect/editor split is the canonical shape — an expensive reasoning model plans, a cheaper model with its own edit format applies — a documented cost/quality win. Roo Code's Orchestrator returned a condensed SUMMARY to the parent rather than a transcript to keep the orchestrator's context small; Codex CLI subagents return prose summaries for the same reason. Claude Code's finalize turn already resumes a session by id internally, exactly as weft's adapters do. What none of them offers is the handoff as a typed, journaled, replay-safe edge between two schema-validated steps.
risks: The deepest risk is a determinism illusion: a resumed session carries vendor-side state the journal does not describe, so a fresh replay of the same journal on a machine where the session has expired takes the digest path and can produce a different answer for the second step. That is why the fallback must be journaled as a divergence-adjacent attempt rather than silently swallowed, and why `onHandoffLost: "fail"` must exist for workflows needing the stronger guarantee. Secondary: a long resumed session may already be near its context limit, so the second step can fail on max turns in ways a fresh session would not.
fitsArchitecture: `sdk/src/types.ts` (`continueFrom`, `onHandoffLost`), `core/src/provider.ts` (`AgentRequest.resume`), `core/src/ctx.ts` (payload `continuesFrom`, digest assembly from the journaled transcript blob via the existing `loadOutput`/blob path, fallback attempt journaling), `provider-claude/src/index.ts` (pass `resume` on the initial stream, not just repair/finalize), `provider-codex/src/index.ts` (`resumeThread` on the initial turn), `testing/` (the conformance suite above already asserts resume semantics).

title: ctx.memory — a durable, journal-honest knowledge store across runs
problem: Every weft run starts from nothing. A write step's worktree is seeded from the integration commit and handed to an agent with no accumulated understanding of the repository — which modules are owned by whom, which tests are flaky, which refactor was already attempted and rejected last week, what a previous run's `ctx.note` recorded. The journal holds all of it, per run, and then it is inert: nothing reads a prior run's journal into a later run. The determinism gate correctly forbids the obvious workaround, and nothing makes an out-of-band read replayable.
proposal: Add `ctx.memory`, a repo-scoped, namespaced store whose READS are journaled sideeffect steps and whose WRITES land in a separate `.weft/memory` store plus a `memory.written` journal event. Journaling the read result is the crux: a replay serves the recalled value from the journal, so a run stays reproducible even after the memory store has moved on — memory becomes a source of nondeterminism domesticated exactly the way `ctx.now`/`ctx.random` already are. Entries are schema-validated on write (the same Zod path as everything else), carry the `runId` that produced them as provenance, and `recall` takes a namespace plus a substring/prefix query (the sqlite index already implements a LIKE scan that can back it). Add `weft memory ls|get|rm` and a `weft run --fresh` flag that makes every `recall` return empty, so a clean-room reproduction is one flag away.
priorArt: LangGraph separates thread-scoped checkpoints from a cross-thread `store` for long-term memory — "Stores persist application-defined data outside the graph state" — precisely this split. Cloudflare Agents give each Durable Object its own private SQLite queried with `this.sql`. Google ADK uses state key scope prefixes (`app:`, `user:`, `temp:`) so persistence lifetime is declared at the key, and `temp:` is never persisted — a directly stealable idea for secrets and huge blobs. None of them journals the read, which is what makes weft's version replay-safe rather than merely persistent.
risks: Memory is the most direct threat to weft's core promise: a run whose behaviour depends on mutable out-of-band state is not reproducible unless the read is journaled, and it is easy to add a convenience API (a synchronous cache, a helper that peeks) that quietly breaks that. The API must have exactly one read path and it must be a step. Second, memory becomes an unaudited prompt-injection channel — a `remember` written by an agent in run A is prompt text handed to an agent in run B — so entries need provenance (present), schema validation (present), and a `weft memory ls` a human can actually read. Third, no blob GC story exists today and memory would inherit that problem, hence `ttl`.
fitsArchitecture: `sdk/src/types.ts` (MemoryApi on Ctx), `core/src/stores.ts` (a `MemoryStore` interface beside JournalStore/BlobStore, with an in-memory implementation for `runWorkflow`), `store-fs/src/memory.ts` (JSONL per namespace, same locked-append discipline as the journal), `core/src/ctx.ts` (recall/remember as journaled sideeffect steps), `core/src/events.ts` (`memory.written`), `index-sqlite/src/` (optional index so `query` is more than a scan), `host/src/weft.ts` (wire the store, `--fresh`), new `cli/src/commands/memory.ts`, `testing/src/run.ts` (memory fixtures).

title: AGENTS.md ingestion as a journaled context step
problem: AGENTS.md is now read by Codex, Claude Code, Copilot, Cursor, Aider, Jules, VS Code and goose — 60,000+ repositories, under Linux Foundation AAIF governance. weft reads none of it. A weft write step hands an agent a freshly created worktree stripped of every convention the same repository's other agents receive by default: build commands, test commands, code style, security notes. The agent then rediscovers them expensively or ignores them badly. This is free ecosystem interop that weft is currently declining.
proposal: Add `ctx.context.repo({ for })`, a journaled sideeffect step that collects AGENTS.md files with nearest-wins precedence (the convention's own rule) and returns their concatenated text plus the list of files read. Agent steps gain `context: "auto" | "none" | string[]` — `"auto"` (opt-in, not default, for one release) prepends the collected guidance for the step's write scope, or the repo root for a read-only step. The crucial design choice: the collected TEXT does not enter the step's identity payload — only the mode does — so editing AGENTS.md does not invalidate every journaled step in the repository; but because the collection is itself a journaled step whose result is served on replay, a resumed run still sees exactly the guidance the first pass saw. `weft doctor` reports which files it found.
priorArt: AGENTS.md itself — originated by OpenAI Codex, now an AAIF/Linux Foundation project, honoured by Codex, Claude Code, GitHub Copilot coding agent, Google Jules, goose, Cursor and Aider, with nested nearest-wins precedence and an explicit user prompt overriding the file. Google ADK's per-directory scoping and Roo Code's project-committable custom modes are the same instinct applied to configuration rather than prose.
risks: AGENTS.md is prose from the repository, and in a repo accepting outside contributions it is a prompt-injection surface — a malicious PR editing AGENTS.md changes what every subsequent agent is told. Mitigations: journal the sources so an audit is possible, and treat the collected text as untrusted (the MCP spec's stance on tool descriptions applies verbatim). Secondary: the guidance inflates every prompt in a wide fan-out, which interacts with the prefix-cache idea — collected context is exactly the shared prefix worth declaring as `cachePrefix`.
fitsArchitecture: `sdk/src/types.ts` (ContextApi on Ctx, `AgentOptions.context`), `core/src/ctx.ts` (the collection step; prepend before the existing write-scope paragraph at ctx.ts:485-493), `core/src/config.ts` + `host/src/config.ts` (`context.files`, `context.default`), `cli/src/commands/doctor.ts`. No gate change: this is plain fs reading inside an engine-owned step, not workflow code.

title: Live step-progress channel: see inside a running agent step
problem: An agent step is a black box for its entire duration — which, at `limits.stepTimeoutMs` default of 20 minutes, is a long time. Both adapters already accumulate transcript lines as the stream arrives (`assistant:`, `assistant → tool: <name>`, `exec (<status>): <cmd>`, `files (<status>): <kind> <path>`) and throw all of it away until the step completes and the transcript is written to a blob. So `weft --watch` re-renders a tree every 500ms in which the interesting node just says "running", the daemon's SSE stream carries journal records only (nothing is journaled mid-step), and there is no way to distinguish a working step from a hung one short of waiting for the timeout.
proposal: Add an `emit` callback to `RunControl` and a per-run in-memory progress bus in the engine. Adapters call `ctl.emit({ kind: "tool", name, target })` / `{ kind: "text", text }` from the same place they already push transcript lines — a one-line change per adapter, since the fold functions exist. The bus is a bounded ring buffer per run, deliberately NOT journaled: the rate is too high and it would double journal size for data the transcript blob already preserves at completion. `engine.progress(runId)` returns an async iterator; the daemon adds `event: progress` to its existing SSE stream and the UI shows the active step's last few lines and the files it is touching; `weft --watch` renders the same under the active tree node. An opt-in `progress: "journal"` per step journals a decimated digest (one record per tool call, capped) for cases where after-the-fact forensics matter more than journal size.
priorArt: Agent Client Protocol (Zed) streams tool-call updates carrying status AND the file locations touched, which is what turns a log wall into supervision — and it makes diffs a first-class streamed content block. Claude Code's `/workflows` TUI drills into any agent's live prompt and tool calls. Mastra ships resumable output streams (`run.resumeStream()`) so a client dropping mid-run reattaches without losing chunks. Linear's Agent Sessions require an acknowledgement within 10 seconds specifically so a human can tell "thinking" from "hung".
risks: The temptation to journal this is the risk: doing so would inflate journals by an order of magnitude for data the transcript blob already holds, and make replay fold cost proportional to chatter rather than to steps. Keeping it non-journaled means progress is lost on a crash — acceptable, and the honest framing. Second, `emit` is a new obligation on adapters, so it must be optional (`emit?`) and the conformance suite must not require it. Third, progress text can contain repository secrets; the daemon is loopback-only today, but this is one more reason the redaction gap on step outputs matters.
fitsArchitecture: `core/src/provider.ts` (RunControl.emit, ProviderProgress), `core/src/engine.ts` (per-run ring buffer + `progress()`), `core/src/ctx.ts` (pass `emit` through `StepIO` into `runProviderWithRepair`), `provider-claude/src/index.ts` and `provider-codex/src/transcript.ts` (emit alongside existing transcript folds), `daemon/src/app.ts` + `ui.ts` (SSE event type + render), `cli/src/outcome.ts` + `format.ts` (active-node line in the live frame).

title: stdlib: escalate() — a cost ladder with a declared acceptance test
problem: weft has per-step routing and hard USD ceilings but no shipped pattern that uses one to protect the other. Today the author picks a model per call site at authoring time, which means either paying Opus prices for steps a Haiku could have done, or discovering the cheap model was insufficient only when a downstream check fails and the run is already over budget. The stdlib's six patterns forward only provider/model/effort (`internal.ts` Routing) and none of them expresses "try cheap, verify, escalate".
proposal: Ship `escalate(ctx, opts)`: an ordered ladder of routings for the SAME prompt and schema, with a caller-supplied `accept` predicate deciding whether a rung's answer is good enough. Each rung is a distinct keyed step (`fix:auth@0`, `fix:auth@1`) so salvage works per rung and a resume does not re-pay for a rung that already ran and was rejected — the rejection itself is journaled as a `drop` with its reason. `accept` is ordinary workflow code, so the natural predicate is a `ctx.check` or a cheap judge step. The pattern reports which rung won so the report can show a per-workflow escalation rate — the signal an author needs to move the default rung down.
priorArt: Aider's architect/editor split is per-role routing with a demonstrated cost/quality win (expensive model plans, cheap model applies). DSPy's `TwoStepAdapter` runs a strong model freely and a small model to extract structure. goose's recipe `retry { max_retries, checks }` binds shell-command acceptance tests to a run, which is the `accept` half — but as a whole-run retry with no ladder. Nobody ships the combination of a cost ladder, a declared acceptance test, and per-rung journaled identity.
risks: The obvious failure mode is spending MORE than a single expensive call: three rungs that all fail cost the sum. The pattern should refuse to escalate when remaining budget cannot cover the next rung — which needs a small read-only budget accessor on Ctx that does not exist today (`ctx.budget.remaining()`), derived from journaled state so it stays replay-safe. Second, `accept` running a real `ctx.check` per rung multiplies exec cost, so the pattern must key its checks per rung or replay re-runs them.
fitsArchitecture: New `stdlib/src/escalate.ts` plus exports in `stdlib/src/index.ts`, using the existing `routing()` and `prefixed()` helpers from `stdlib/src/internal.ts`. One small core addition: a read-only `ctx.budget` view (`{ remainingTokens, remainingUsd, spent }`) in `sdk/src/types.ts` and `core/src/ctx.ts`, derived from the existing `Budget` — which the determinism gate is fine with because it is engine state, not a banned global.

title: stdlib: bestOfPatch() — N candidate patches, verified in their own worktrees, judged on evidence
problem: weft has the only assembly in the landscape that could make best-of-N rigorous for code — per-attempt worktrees, captured patches as typed values, `ctx.check`, and a gated `ctx.integrate()` — and ships none of it. `judgePanel` exists but judges prose: it spawns one judge per surviving attempt (count not configurable), shows attempts in fixed index order with no anonymisation, and has no notion of a patch or a check. So the highest-value use of parallel isolated worktrees — run the same fix three ways, keep the one that actually passes the tests — must be hand-written, and the hard part is not expressible at all: `ctx.check` runs in `rt.cwd`, and a write step's worktree is torn down in its `finally`.
proposal: Two pieces. Core: add `ctx.verify(result, checkOpts)` — a journaled step that re-materialises a captured patch into a scratch worktree (`applyPatchToTree` already exists in `isolation`), runs the check there, and attaches the result to the patch as evidence, without touching the integration tree.
