Stdlib: `bestOfPatch(ctx, opts)` fans out N write steps against the same scope with varied routing, `ctx.verify`s each, discards candidates whose required check fails, and only then runs a judge among the survivors — with candidate order shuffled by `ctx.random()` (journaled, so replay reproduces the order) to blunt the position bias `judgePanel` currently has. It returns the winner's `DetailedAgentResult` ready for `ctx.integrate()` and calls `ctx.discard()` on the losers so the run cannot end with `unintegrated_patches`.
priorArt: Crystal (now Nimbalyst) was built explicitly for running several attempts at one task and comparing them, with per-session run scripts to verify a change before merging. uzi launched dozens of agents on one task from a single command and died precisely because it had no way to evaluate them — human comparison of 20 diffs does not scale. Braintrust's autoevals ships pairwise `Battle` scoring because absolute quality scores for code are close to meaningless. VoltAgent's `andRace` is the speculative-execution cousin. weft's contribution is that selection can be evidence-based (a real check inside the candidate's own tree) rather than a judge's opinion.
risks: Cost multiplies by N by construction, so the pattern must interact with the budget: it should refuse to fan out when remaining headroom cannot cover N candidates plus verification, using the same `ctx.budget` view `escalate` needs. `ctx.verify` re-materialising a patch is a real correctness surface — the scratch worktree must be seeded from the same `integrationBaseCommit` the candidate was seeded from, or the check runs against a different world than the patch expects, and a conflict there must be reported as an inconclusive verification rather than a failure. Disk pressure from N+1 simultaneous worktrees on a laptop is genuine (SWE-agent had to add startup jitter for exactly this) and argues for the pattern honouring a concurrency cap.
fitsArchitecture: `core/src/ctx.ts` (`ctx.verify` — a journaled step reusing `integrationBaseCommit`, `addWorktree`/`removeWorktree` from `isolation/src/worktree.ts` and `applyPatchToTree` from `isolation/src/patch.ts`), `sdk/src/types.ts` (Ctx.verify), `core/src/events.ts` (the check event already carries evidence; add the patch key), new `stdlib/src/best-of.ts` + `stdlib/src/index.ts` exports, and a shared shuffle helper in `stdlib/src/internal.ts` that `judgePanel` should adopt too.

title: Self-improving workflows: a journal-mined hint bank with human-reviewed prompt patches
problem: weft journals every schema-repair attempt (`step.attempt "schema repair n/max"`), every `schema_repair_exhausted`, every failed required check, every scope violation and every `drop`, across every run in `.weft/runs`. That is a dense, structured corpus of exactly where each prompt is failing — and nothing reads it. Each run repeats the previous run's mistakes at full price, and an author discovers a systematically bad prompt only by noticing a pattern by eye. Meanwhile the sqlite index is never updated incrementally (nothing in core calls `indexRun`), so even the raw material is stale between manual rebuilds.
proposal: Two halves, deliberately split so the automatic part is safe and the risky part stays human. (1) A hint bank: when a step's repair loop fires or a required check fails, the engine records `{ stepKey, schemaHash, issuePath, message }` into the memory store. On a later run a step opting into `hints: true` has the top-K recurring hints for its key rendered into the prompt — and, crucially, the rendered hints go INTO the identity payload, so a run with different hints is honestly a different step rather than a silent behavioural change hiding behind the same hash. (2) A `weft optimize <workflow>` verb that folds every journal for that workflow, clusters recurring failures by (stepKey, issuePath), and emits a DIFF against the workflow source — a proposed prompt edit with supporting evidence and a measured failure rate — for a human to review in git. It never writes the file. This keeps the loop DSPy automates under review, which is the right trade for code that mutates repositories.
priorArt: DSPy's optimizers (MIPROv2, GEPA reflective prompt evolution, BootstrapFewShot) automatically search instructions and few-shot demos against a metric — nobody else in the landscape automates prompt improvement, and DSPy's compiled programs serialize to JSON as versionable artefacts. Opik's Agent Optimizer wires the same idea into a trace/eval store. Braintrust's agentbehavior specifies trajectory-level behaviour so the process is supervised, not only the outcome. Google ADK's `adk conformance` shows the complementary guard: a golden recording that fails CI on deviation, which would keep an optimizer's edits honest.
risks: The largest is a feedback loop that degrades quality invisibly: hints derived from a handful of runs are noise, and injecting them makes the next run's failures correlated with the hints rather than with the prompt — so the bank must require a minimum support count and stay inspectable (`weft memory ls weft:hints`). Putting hints in the identity hash is correct but means enabling them invalidates a workflow's journal history once, which needs a loud divergence reason. The optimizer half must never auto-apply, and its `--json` output must not become a CI job committing prompt edits without review: the corpus that suggests a good edit will also suggest a bad one, and a prompt edit changes what an agent does to a repository. Finally this depends on `ctx.memory` (or an equivalent store) existing and on the sqlite index actually being maintained.
fitsArchitecture: Depends on the memory store from the `ctx.memory` idea (`core/src/stores.ts`, `store-fs/src/memory.ts`). `core/src/ctx.ts` (record hints in the repair loop and check-failure path; render them into the payload when `hints: true`), `sdk/src/types.ts` (`AgentOptions.hints`), new `cli/src/commands/optimize.ts` (folds journals via the existing `JournalStore.list`/`read`, clusters, emits a unified diff — pure analysis, no engine changes), `index-sqlite/src/run-index.ts` (a repairs/checks table so clustering is a query rather than a full re-fold), `host/src/weft.ts` (call `indexRun` incrementally so the corpus is not stale).

title: Notifier seam: make a durable gate reach a person
problem: Verified by grep across packages/*/src: there is no Slack, email, webhook, or push code anywhere in the repo. A `human.requested` event lands in the journal and the run parks durably — but the only ways to discover it are running `weft status`, opening the loopback-only daemon page on 127.0.0.1:4781, or holding an MCP `weft_wait` long-poll. The README's promise that "the answer can arrive hours later" is true in mechanism and hollow in practice: durability solves waiting, not noticing. Every other capability weft has (budget ceilings, patch quarantine, timeout policies) assumes a human eventually shows up.
proposal: Add `@techery/weft-notify`: a `Notifier` interface plus a journal-tailing dispatcher the host wires in. The dispatcher subscribes to `engine.watch(runId)` (already public, engine.ts:1778) for every active run and to `store.list()` for runs it did not start, and fans `human.requested`, `human.rejected`, `run.failed`, `run.completed`, and `budget.sampled`-crossing-a-threshold to configured channels. `HumanRequestEvent` already carries everything a message needs — id, kind, question, detail, artifactRef, schema, risk, deadline, onTimeout, confirmToken. Delivery is at-least-once and idempotent on `(runId, requestId, channel)` recorded in a small `.weft/notified.jsonl` sidecar so a daemon restart does not re-spam. Ship three built-ins — `webhook` (POST the event plus a deep link), `slack` (chat.postMessage with Block Kit and the exact `weft answer` command in a code block), `desktop` (node-notifier) — and a `command` channel that shells out so anyone can add one in five lines. Config is a new top-level strict section in `packages/host/src/config.ts`, and because `human.answered` already carries `channel?: string` and `Engine.answer` already accepts `{ channel }` (engine.ts:1347), a reply that comes back through a channel is journaled with its provenance for free.
priorArt: HumanLayer routes each approval through a contact-channel object carrying human-readable context about who is being asked, with escalation ladders and timeouts. Windmill's getResumeUrls() mails signed approval links and ships native Slack/Teams interactive approvals. Trigger.dev's wait.createToken() returns a webhook URL plus tags so pending approvals are filterable. Temporal, Vercel WDK, Mastra and LangGraph all have durable pause primitives and none has a delivery channel — the same gap, equally load-bearing.
risks: Bot tokens in config invite the same secret-handling problem ctx.secret solves for workflows — the config must take an env var name, never a literal, and the notifier must run outside the determinism sandbox (it is host code, not workflow code, so the AST gate does not apply, but that boundary needs to be explicit or someone will try to call it from a step). At-least-once delivery means duplicate Slack messages after a crash; the sidecar dedup file is another thing that can rot. Notification volume on a 40-way fan-out with per-step gates is a self-inflicted DoS, so per-run coalescing is required from day one, not later.
fitsArchitecture: New leaf package `packages/notify` depending only on sdk types plus the core event union. `packages/host/src/config.ts` gains a strict `notify` section (the top-level schema is already `.loose()`, so older hosts ignore it). `packages/host/src/weft.ts` constructs the dispatcher and `close()` stops it. `packages/cli` gains `weft notify test`. `packages/core` changes not at all — the dispatcher is a pure consumer of `engine.watch()` and the store.

title: Gate bridge: answer a weft gate from a GitHub PR, Linear issue, or Slack thread
problem: Even with notifications, answering requires a terminal on the machine holding the journal, or a browser on 127.0.0.1. `weft answer` is a durable, CAS-guarded, schema-validating entry point (engine.ts:1343-1467, with cross-descendant routing at :1476) — it is genuinely the best-engineered answer path in the landscape and it is reachable from exactly one shell. Meanwhile the run that raised the gate is usually about a specific PR or ticket, and the reviewer is already looking at that PR.
proposal: Add `@techery/weft-bridge`: a long-lived process (or a GitHub Action step) that renders a pending request into the surface where the work lives and folds the reply back through `Engine.answer(runId, requestId, value, { channel: "github:PR#412" })`. Three adapters. GitHub: post a sticky comment on the PR carrying the question, the risk tier, the rendered artifact (a `review` step's artifactRef blob is markdown or a diff — render it as a collapsed `<details>` fenced block), and a checklist of options derived from the journaled JSON Schema; a reply comment matching `/^@weft (approve|deny|<json>)/` becomes the answer. Linear: implement the Agent Session shape — the run is a delegate on the issue, `human.requested` renders as an elicitation activity, the reply in-thread is the answer. Slack: Block Kit buttons for enum/boolean schemas, a modal for object schemas, falling back to a JSON code block. Every adapter validates through the same journaled JSON Schema `structuralCheck` already applies to out-of-process answers (jsonschema.ts:86), so a malformed reply is refused at the edge and the reject-and-reopen loop (runtime.ts:959-994) still owns the authoritative check. Replies carry a signed capability token so an arbitrary commenter cannot approve an irreversible gate; the `confirmToken` weft already mints for irreversible+ask is echoed by the bridge only when the replier is on a configured allowlist.
priorArt: Linear Agent Sessions renders elicitation as an activity inline in the issue thread that motivated the work, with the agent as delegate rather than assignee so accountability stays with a human. OpenAI Codex Cloud initiates tasks and delivers results through GitHub PRs, GitLab MRs, Linear issues and Slack. Claude Code Action posts a live-updating checklist comment in the issue/PR thread (presentation only — no mid-run gate). Windmill ships native interactive Slack and Teams approvals with N-of-M and no-self-approval.
risks: This is the highest-value idea here and also the one that most easily becomes an unauthenticated approve button for anyone with comment access on a public repo — the approver allowlist and token signing are not a v2 concern. Rendering an arbitrary Zod schema into Block Kit or a checkbox list is a long tail that will fall back to raw JSON more often than the demo suggests. Each adapter is an ongoing API-drift tax (three vendors, three auth models). Bridging a `review` step means posting a diff into a comment, which needs size limits and secret scrubbing before it goes anywhere public — and step outputs are journaled verbatim today (see the redaction idea).
fitsArchitecture: New package `packages/bridge` consuming `engine.pending()`, `engine.watch()`, and `engine.answer()` — all already public and already designed for out-of-process callers, including the descendant-routing that finds which child run actually owns a request id (engine.ts:993-1046). `packages/host/src/config.ts` gains a `bridge` section. `packages/cli` gains `weft bridge`. Zero changes to core: the `channel` provenance slot on `human.answered` was clearly built for exactly this and is currently written only by the daemon (app.ts:165).

title: `weft conformance`: pin a run's agent trace as a golden file and fail CI when it drifts
problem: weft can prove a step returned the declared shape and can say nothing about whether the output was any good or whether the run took the expected path. The journal is already a complete, structured recording of every model interaction — prompt, route, schema, usage, repair attempts, the exact sequence of steps — and it is used only for crash recovery. Meanwhile `runWorkflow` requires hand-written `mock().on(...)` fixtures for every agent step, which is real authoring friction and means a workflow edit that reorders steps or changes a prompt passes CI silently as long as the fixtures still match by glob.
proposal: Two commands over the existing journal. `weft conformance record <workflow> --args ...` runs the workflow for real once and writes `.weft/conformance/<name>.json`: for each agent step, the resolved prompt, route, schema hash, and the validated output, keyed by the step's canonical content hash (canonical.ts already computes exactly this identity). `weft conformance check` re-runs the workflow against a new `ReplayAgentProvider` — a real `AgentProvider` registered under the `claude`/`codex` ids, so the run exercises the genuine routing, budget, journaling, scope-checking and integrate paths with zero model calls — and diffs the resulting journal's step sequence and outputs against the golden file. Divergence classes are reported separately and separately gated: `step-added`, `step-removed`, `step-reordered`, `prompt-changed`, `schema-changed`, `output-changed`. A `--update` flag re-records. This also becomes the corpus replay gate the self-review flagged as missing: `weft conformance check --replay` runs `engine.replayDry()` over every recorded journal and fails on unexpected divergence — which incidentally forces fixing `replayDry`'s three known infidelities (it skips positionsTrusted, ignores opts.defHash, and resets the budget and agent counter, engine.ts:1792-1827), because the gate is worthless while the tool models a different world than a real resume.
priorArt: Google ADK's `adk conformance` records a scenario's LLM requests, responses and tool calls into generated-recordings.yaml + generated-session.yaml golden baselines, then defaults to Replay Mode where any deviation fails the command — explicitly designed to block a PR. Temporal's Worker.runReplayHistory() feeds recorded production histories through new code and throws DeterminismViolationError, which is the same idea for the durability axis. AutoGen's ReplayChatCompletionClient is the cleanest framing of the mechanism: make the stub a provider, not a test mode, so tests exercise the real routing and budget code paths.
risks: Golden files rot: a prompt change is usually intentional, so if `--update` is the reflex the gate degrades into noise. Divergence classes must be individually configurable (fail on step-added, warn on prompt-changed) or teams will disable it. Recording a real run costs real money and captures whatever the model said that day, so a golden file is a sample, not a specification — the check must be about the workflow's shape and the model's contract, not about the exact prose of an output. `verifyServe` is disabled whenever testHooks are configured (ctx.ts:1501), so a conformance run still would not exercise the effect-still-holds re-check; that exclusion needs narrowing to git hooks specifically.
fitsArchitecture: `packages/testing` gains `replayProvider` and the golden-trace reader/writer, exported alongside the existing conformance suites (it already has a separate `/conformance` subpath entry so vitest stays an optional peer). `packages/cli` gains the `conformance` command. `packages/host` gains a `conformance` provider-registration mode next to the existing `--mock` mode in weft.ts:94-110 — the same seam, a different builder. Core is untouched except for the `replayDry` fidelity fixes in `packages/core/src/engine.ts`.

title: Per-step OpenTelemetry spans with OpenInference span kinds
problem: Verified: `packages/core/src/engine.ts:789` is the only `tracer.startSpan` in the repo — one span per run, run id as trace id. weft's journal is the richest per-step record in this whole landscape (kind, key, phase, route, effort, per-attempt usage in/out/cached, USD, repair attempts, scope violations, gate decisions, patch refs, childRunId) and none of it is legible to any tool a team already runs. The README lists this as a known deviation. Every competing platform's trace UI is a build weft does not need to do, if it emits standard spans.
proposal: Add `@techery/weft-otel`: a pure fold from journal records to spans, usable two ways. Live: an `EngineObserver` the host attaches that opens a span on `step.scheduled` and ends it on `step.completed`/`step.failed`, nesting by the `parentSeq` the journal already records via AsyncLocalStorage. Retro: `weft otel export <run>` re-folds a finished journal into an OTLP batch, so runs that happened before anyone configured a collector are still exportable. Attributes follow the OTel GenAI semantic conventions — `gen_ai.operation.name` (`invoke_agent` for agent steps, `execute_tool` for exec/bash/fetch/git, `chat` for the provider call), `gen_ai.provider.name`, `gen_ai.request.model`, and the token breakdown including `gen_ai.usage.cache_read.input_tokens` which weft already collects and which its USD ceiling arguably needs to price correctly — plus OpenInference `openinference.span.kind` so a Phoenix/Langfuse UI renders each node purposefully. weft already knows every step's kind; mapping `agent`→LLM, `check`→EVALUATOR, `gate`/`human`→GUARDRAIL, `workflow`→CHAIN, `exec`/`bash`/`git`→TOOL is a switch statement. Message content is opt-in and passes through a redaction pass (see the redaction idea) before it ever leaves the process.
priorArt: Arize Phoenix's OpenInference span kinds (LLM/CHAIN/TOOL/AGENT/RETRIEVER/GUARDRAIL/EVALUATOR) give a UI enough type information to render each node purposefully — the exact vocabulary weft's journal already has and does not emit. Langfuse is OTel-native with typed span/generation/event and cost from a maintained pricing table. Opik treats first-party OTLP ingest as a peer to its SDKs. Mastra emits OTel AI tracing with auto-derived cost metrics. The OTel GenAI conventions themselves now define invoke_agent and execute_tool operations plus the cache-read/reasoning token breakouts.
risks: The GenAI conventions are still in Development status, so attribute names will move — pinning a convention version in config and keeping the mapping in one file is the mitigation. OpenInference and the official conventions are competing dialects; emitting both sets of attributes on the same span is ugly but works and is what the ecosystem currently does. Content capture is the real hazard: weft's spans would carry source code and diffs from private repos, so `captureContent` must default to `off`, not `redacted`. Live span emission on a 4096-wide fan-out is a lot of spans — sampling belongs in the config from the start.
fitsArchitecture: New leaf package `packages/otel` importing only the core event union and `@opentelemetry/api` (already a core dependency). Core exposes an `EngineObserver` hook or the existing `onRecords` path is reused; either way the single run-level span at engine.ts:789 becomes the root of a real tree rather than the whole tree. `packages/host` wires it from config; `packages/cli` adds `weft otel export`.

title: Machine-readable CLI: `--json` on every verb, plus the four missing commands
problem: All 14 commands emit ANSI-painted human text only — `grep` for `--json` across packages/cli/src returns nothing. For a tool whose entire pitch is unattended, durable, hours-long runs, being unscriptable is a structural adoption blocker: putting weft in CI means parsing terminal output. The gaps compound: there is no `weft signal` even though the daemon exposes POST /api/runs/:id/signal (app.ts:174) with no CLI peer; no `reindex` or `search` even though `packages/index-sqlite` implements `search()` and `weft.reindex()` exists (weft.ts:138); no way to view a step transcript or a captured patch blob (`explain` prints patchRef as a bare string); no `--version`.
proposal: Define one JSON view module in the CLI shared by every command and by the daemon's REST responses, so `weft status --json` and `GET /api/runs/:id` return the same shape and a script written against one works against the other. Add `--json` to ls, status, report, explain, diff, replay --dry, check, doctor, and conformance. Add the four missing verbs: `weft signal <run> <name> [json]` (thin wrapper over `engine.signal`, already public at engine.ts:1536); `weft search <query>` and `weft reindex` over the sqlite index that already exists and is currently reachable from no host at all; `weft cat <run> <step> [--patch|--transcript|--output]` resolving blob refs through the blob store so a patch or transcript can be piped to `git apply` or `less`; and `--version` on the program. Exit codes become a documented contract: 0 success, 1 failure, 2 suspended-on-human, 3 budget-exceeded — so a CI step can branch on "needs a human" without parsing anything.
priorArt: Temporal, Restate (`restate invocations pause/resume`) and Trigger.dev all ship CLI verbs designed for automation rather than for reading. gh-aw compiles to a checked-in artifact CI consumes directly. Braintrust runs evals through a CLI whose output a GitHub Action turns into PR comments. This is table stakes everywhere else in the landscape.
risks: A JSON shape is an API the moment someone scripts against it, so it needs a `schemaVersion` field on day one and the same strictness weft applies to its config. Sharing the view module with the daemon is right but couples cli and daemon release cadence unless the types live in sdk. `weft cat --patch` streams repo content to stdout, which is fine locally and is exactly the thing that must not be piped into a bridge comment without scrubbing.
fitsArchitecture: Almost entirely `packages/cli`: a new `src/json.ts` view module, `--json` flags on existing commands, four new files under `src/commands/`. The shared view types belong in `packages/sdk` so `packages/daemon` can import them without depending on the CLI. `weft search`/`reindex` finally give `packages/index-sqlite` a host — today nothing in cli, mcp or daemon references it. Core is untouched; every verb already has a public Engine method.

title: Repo-root discovery, blob GC, and `weft doctor --fix`
problem: Three small things that each make weft feel like a preview. (1) Verified: `--cwd` defaults to `process.cwd()` and `.weft` is always `<cwd>/.weft` with no walk toward a parent (context.ts:24, weft.ts:85), so running any command from a subdirectory of the repo silently targets a different, empty `.weft` and reports "no runs" instead of erroring — every git-adjacent tool on earth walks upward. (2) `BlobStore` exposes only put/get/getText/has (stores.ts:88-93), so transcripts, patches, review artifacts and every step output over the 64KB threshold accumulate forever under `.weft/blobs` with no prune verb and no retention policy. (3) `weft doctor` diagnoses nine things and fixes none of them.
proposal: (1) Walk upward from `--cwd` for the nearest directory containing `.weft` or `.git`, stopping at the filesystem root; print the resolved root in `weft doctor` and on `--verbose`; keep an explicit `--cwd` as an override that disables the walk. Add a doctor check that fails loudly when the resolved root differs from the invocation directory in a way the user probably did not intend. (2) Add `weft prune`: mark-and-sweep over `.weft/runs/*/journal.jsonl` collecting every `$outputBlob`, `patch.captured` ref, transcript ref and artifactRef, then delete unreferenced blobs; `--runs <age>` also removes whole runs older than a cutoff (terminal only, never a run with pending requests, never a claimed run) and re-runs `RunIndex.rebuild()`. Add `weft rm <run>`. (3) `weft doctor --fix` creates `.weft/`, creates the workflow dir, writes a default `config.json`, and runs `rebuildProjections()` on any run whose `state.json` is not strictly newer than its journal — the freshness check journal.ts:467-520 already computes exactly that condition and currently only distrusts the projection rather than repairing it.
sketch:
$ cd packages/core && weft ls
  (today)  no runs
  (after)  weft root: /home/user/weft   (found .weft/ 2 levels up)
           7f3a2b1c  review  suspended  2h ago

$ weft prune --dry-run
  blobs:  1,204 total · 318 unreferenced (412 MB) → would delete
  runs:   41 total · 12 terminal older than 30d → kept (pass --runs 30d)

$ weft prune --runs 30d --yes
  deleted 318 blobs (412 MB), 12 runs; reindexed 29 rows

$ weft doctor --fix
  ✓ node 22.14.0
  ✓ git 2.47.0
  ! .weft/config.json missing            → written (defaults)
  ! run 3d9e1f0a projections stale       → rebuilt from journal
  ✗ ANTHROPIC_API_KEY not set            → cannot fix; run `claude login`
  1 problem to fix
priorArt: Repo-root discovery is universal in git-adjacent tooling (git itself, npm, cargo, biome — weft's own biome.json honours .gitignore from the root). Retention policies ship in Trigger.dev, Langfuse and Temporal. `weft doctor --fix` is the shape of `brew doctor` / `flutter doctor --android-licenses`; the projection-rebuild half is already implemented as `rebuildProjections()` (journal.ts:672-691) and simply has no caller in the CLI.
risks: Root discovery changes behaviour for anyone already relying on the current semantics, so it needs to be visible (print the resolved root) rather than silent. Mark-and-sweep GC deleting a blob a concurrently-running resume is about to read is the classic hazard: prune must skip any run with a live owner claim (`acquireRun` state is already on disk as owner.json) and must sweep only blobs older than the oldest active run. `doctor --fix` writing files is a different trust level from `doctor` reading them, so it should never be the default and never touch a run that is claimed.
fitsArchitecture: `packages/cli/src/context.ts` gains the upward walk. `packages/core/src/stores.ts` adds optional `list()`/`delete()` to the BlobStore interface (optional, following the appendIf/acquireRun precedent, so a store without them just refuses to prune). `packages/store-fs/src/blobs.ts` implements them. `packages/cli` gains `prune`, `rm`, and `--fix`. `packages/index-sqlite` gets called by prune for the reindex.

title: `weft fork`: turn the journal from a recovery log into an exploration surface
problem: weft spent enormous engineering effort on an append-only journal with content-addressed step identity, three-tier salvage matching, and a version stamp — and exposes exactly three verbs over it: resume, cancel, and `replay --dry`. There is no fork-from-step, no branch-a-run, no rewind-and-edit-a-recorded-value, no re-run-one-step. When a 40-step run produces a bad plan at step 3, the only options are to resume (which serves the bad plan from the journal) or to start over (which re-pays for steps 1-2). Every checkpoint-based competitor — which has strictly less information than weft does — ships this.
proposal: `weft fork <run> --from <step> [--set <key>=<json>] [--reuse content|key]`. Mechanism: read the source journal, take records up to and including the chosen step's `step.completed`, write them into a NEW run id's journal with a fresh `run.created` carrying `forkedFrom: {runId, seq}` and the current bodyHash/defHash, optionally rewriting the chosen step's output with `--set` (validated against that step's journaled schema before it is written, so a hand-edited value cannot be less valid than a model's). Then resume the new run normally — the existing salvage machinery serves the copied prefix and re-runs everything after it, with no new engine code needed on the replay path. Patches complicate this and must be handled honestly: a forked run inherits the source's `patch.captured` blob refs (blobs are content-addressed and immutable, so sharing them is safe) but any `patch.merged` after the fork point is dropped, and `ctx.integrate`'s verifyServe chain (ctx.ts:2073-2098) already knows how to detect that the tree does not contain a patch it thought it merged. Add `weft fork --bulk --workflow review --failed-at <key>` for the fleet case. `weft diff <a> <b>` already compares two runs by keyed step outputs, so a fork is immediately comparable against its parent.
sketch:
$ weft explain 7f3a2b1c plan
  ✗ plan  seq 3  phase discover  claude/claude-opus-5  $0.42
  output: { "files": ["src/api.ts"], "strategy": "rewrite everything" }

$ weft fork 7f3a2b1c --from plan --set 'output.strategy="minimal diff"'
  forked 7f3a2b1c@3 → 9c1f0a2d  (3 steps copied, $0.61 preserved)
  validated against the step's journaled schema ✓
  run: weft resume 9c1f0a2d

$ weft fork 7f3a2b1c --from plan --reuse key      # same prefix, re-run the rest live
$ weft diff 7f3a2b1c 9c1f0a2d
  review:src/api.ts   findings: 7 → 2
  3 of 14 step(s) differ

$ weft fork --bulk --workflow review --failed-at 'check:tests' --yes
  forked 12 runs from their last good step
priorArt: DBOS Transact's forkWorkflow(workflowID, startStep, {newWorkflowID, applicationVersion, replacementChildren}) is the best operator verb in the landscape, with bulk fork from the Conductor UI turning "4,000 runs are wedged at step 7" into a UI action. LangGraph's update_state() writes a new checkpoint on the parent and invoking with a checkpoint_id forks an alternate timeline, exposed in Studio as rewind/edit/re-run. Burr makes (app_id, partition_key, sequence_id) a universal fork address. CrewAI Flows distinguishes restore_from_state_id (fork, fresh state.id, parent lineage preserved) from kickoff(inputs={'id'}) (resume, extend) — a thoughtful API split worth copying.
risks: Forking past a step that had external side effects (a push, a PR, an integrate) produces a run whose journal claims things about the world that are no longer true — this is precisely what verifyServe exists for, but most git writes have no verifier (add, fetch, pull, push, reset, apply, stash.*, clean), so `fork --from` past one of those must warn loudly and probably refuse without `--force`. `--set` lets a human write a value the model never produced, which is a feature for debugging and a footgun for anyone treating the journal as an audit trail — the forked record must be marked with its provenance, not silently substituted. Bulk fork is a lot of concurrent runs; it needs the same admission control as fan-out.
fitsArchitecture: Mostly `packages/cli` plus one new `Engine.fork(runId, opts)` in `packages/core/src/engine.ts` that does the journal copy and the schema-validated rewrite; the resume path needs no changes because the forked journal is an ordinary journal. `run.created` in `packages/core/src/events.ts` gains an optional `forkedFrom`. `packages/store-fs` needs nothing new. `packages/daemon` gets a fork button once the verb exists.

title: Cross-run gate inbox: one queue of everything waiting on a person
problem: Pending requests are per-run everywhere in the surface: `weft status <run>` prints them, `GET /api/runs/:id/pending` returns them, `Engine.pending(runId)` takes a run id. There is no way to ask "what is waiting on me right now, across every run in this repo?" — which is the only question a human actually has. `weft ls --status suspended` gets close but does not show the question, the risk, the deadline, or how long it has been blocked, and the daemon's run sidebar shows status but not what any run is blocked on.
proposal: Add `Engine.inbox(filter?)`: fold every run's journal (or read the sqlite index, which already stores human questions in its `search_text` column) into a list of open requests with `{runId, workflow, requestId, kind, question, risk, deadline, waitingMs, answerCommand, owningRunId}` — reusing the descendant-routing logic that already resolves a parent-addressed request to the child that holds it (engine.ts:993-1046). Surface it three ways: `weft inbox [--risk high] [--json] [--overdue]`, `GET /api/pending` in the daemon with the web UI's sidebar gaining an "Inbox" tab that lists open gates across all runs, and a new `weft_pending` MCP tool so a Claude Code session driving weft can ask "anything waiting on me?" without knowing run ids. Sort by deadline proximity so requests about to hit a `deny` timeout float to the top, and show the timeout policy inline — a gate that will auto-deny in 20 minutes is a fundamentally different item from one that will wait forever.

  ⚠ 7f3a2b1c  review          h2  irreversible  merge 12 files into main
                                  waiting 4h12m · auto-DENY in 48m

    9c1f0a2d  audit-and-fix   h1  medium        which conflict resolution?
                                  waiting 22m · no deadline

    3d9e1f0a  review          h4  low           rate this summary (1-5)
                                  waiting 3d · no deadline

$ weft inbox --json --risk high,irreversible | jq -r '.[].answerCommand'

# MCP, from a Claude Code session
> weft_pending {}
{ "pending": [ { "runId": "7f3a2b1c", "id": "h2", "kind": "approve",
                 "question": "merge 12 files into main", "risk": "irreversible",
                 "deadline": 1756...,  "onTimeout": "deny" } ] }
priorArt: Trigger.dev makes waitpoint tokens first-class dashboard objects with tags so pending approvals are filterable and manageable across runs. Windmill's approval pages and Linear's agent-session activities both put pending work in a place the human already looks. GitHub Copilot Agent HQ's mission control is a cross-run view spanning repos. Everything else in the durable-execution cluster — Temporal, WDK, Mastra, LangGraph — is run-scoped like weft and shares the same blind spot.
risks: Folding every journal in `.weft/runs` on every invocation does not scale past a few hundred runs; the sqlite index is the right source but it is only refreshed by a full `RunIndex.rebuild()` today (nothing in core calls indexRun), so either the inbox tolerates staleness or incremental indexing lands first. Requests owned by child runs must be reported under the child's run id (they are run-local) while still being findable from the parent, which the answer path already handles but the listing must not get wrong.
fitsArchitecture: One new method in `packages/core/src/engine.ts` alongside the existing `pending()` and `list()`. `packages/cli` gains `weft inbox`. `packages/daemon/src/app.ts` gains `GET /api/pending` and `src/ui.ts` gains a tab. `packages/mcp/src/tools.ts` gains a `weft_pending` registration marked readOnlyHint, matching the existing seven. Optionally `packages/index-sqlite` gains a `pending()` query so the fold is a SELECT rather than a directory walk.

title: Daemon UI as a real review surface: schema-driven forms, patch diffs, step drill-in
problem: The web UI is one hand-written HTML file (ui.ts:12, INDEX_HTML) whose detail pane is state + tree + pending + report and nothing else. There is no per-step prompt/payload/output view (the CLI's `weft explain` has one and the UI does not), no patch or transcript viewer, no run-to-run diff, no filtering over the run list (the API supports status/workflow/limit and the page always fetches it bare), and the journal tail is capped at 200 records. Answer forms handle one flat level of enum/boolean/string/number and dump everything else into a JSON textarea. Meanwhile `ctx.human.review` exists specifically to put an artifact in front of a person, and the artifact — markdown or a diff, stored as a blob — is rendered as preformatted text.
proposal: Three additions, in priority order. (1) A diff viewer: `human.review` artifacts and `patch.captured` blobs render as a syntax-highlighted, per-hunk diff with the write scope's in-scope/out-of-scope classification shown inline — weft already computes `outOfScope` and `quarantined` on every PatchRef, and showing which hunks fell outside the declared scope is information no other tool has. (2) Step drill-in: clicking a node in the phase tree opens what `weft explain` prints — status, route, effort, attempts, duration, per-attempt usage, the journaled payload with the agent prompt rendered raw, the output (blob-resolved), the patch ref, the child run id — plus a "fork from here" button once `weft fork` exists. (3) A full JSON-Schema form renderer replacing the flat one: arrays with add/remove, nested objects, oneOf as a discriminated selector, with client-side validation against the journaled schema and the existing rebuild-only-when-the-request-set-changes behaviour preserved so a half-typed answer survives a poll. All of it stays a single dependency-free file — the constraint is good and the current implementation proves it is workable at this size.
priorArt: Vibe Kanban's inline diff commenting with a preview browser was the best review UX in the coding-agent cluster (and the project is sunsetting, so the idea is free). Agent Client Protocol makes diff a first-class typed content block precisely so editors render agent changes inline. Windmill renders approval forms from a schema so the reviewer's fields arrive as typed resume values. Burr proves a fully self-hosted OSS tracking UI over every state transition is a real differentiator when every well-funded competitor's good UI is behind a paywall.
risks: A dependency-free single file with a real diff viewer and a schema form renderer is a lot of hand-written JS; the temptation to add a build step will be strong and should be resisted only as long as the file stays readable. Serving blob content over HTTP means the loopback+Origin guard is now protecting repository source code rather than just run metadata, which raises the stakes on the daemon's complete absence of authentication (app.ts:70-80 is the only guard). Rendering an attacker-influenced diff as HTML is an XSS surface — escape everything, no exceptions.
fitsArchitecture: `packages/daemon` only: three routes in `src/app.ts` and the renderer work in `src/ui.ts`. The step-detail route can reuse the same resolution helpers `packages/cli/src/runio.ts` already implements (resolveOutput, payloadOf, findStep) if those move to `packages/sdk` or a shared module. The scope classification is already computed and journaled — `scope.violation` events and `PatchRef.outOfScope` — so the route is a fold, not new logic.

title: CI-native weft: a GitHub Action, PR-comment reports, and gates as review requests
problem: weft's strongest properties — a durable journal, a cost ceiling, a patch that lands only at an explicit integrate — are exactly what a CI-run agent needs, and there is no CI story at all. No action, no documented exit codes, no artifact convention, no way for a workflow blocked on a human to survive the end of a job. A GitHub Actions run that hits `ctx.human.approve` today just sits there until the job times out and loses everything.
proposal: Ship `techery/weft-action` plus the engine-side pieces that make it honest. The action runs `weft run <workflow> --json`, uploads `.weft/runs/<id>/` as a job artifact (journal, blobs, projections), and posts `report.md` as a sticky PR comment. The interesting case is suspension: on exit code 2 the action does NOT fail — it uploads the journal, posts the pending gate as a PR review comment through the bridge, and exits successfully with a `suspended` output. A companion `weft-resume-action` triggered by `issue_comment` downloads the artifact, restores `.weft/runs/<id>/`, delivers the answer via `weft answer`, and resumes — the journal is the entire portable state, which is precisely the property weft has and nobody else in the CI-agent space does. Add `weft run --budget` enforcement as a required input so a runaway CI agent is bounded by construction, and add a `--read-only` mode where the run may capture patches but `ctx.integrate` is refused, so the agent's output is a PR rather than a push (gh-aw's safe-output shape, expressed through machinery weft already has).
sketch:
# .github/workflows/review.yml
- uses: techery/weft-action@v1
  id: weft
  with:
    workflow: review
    args: '{"base":"${{ github.base_ref }}"}'
    budget: '500k,$5'
    read-only: true
    comment: pr        # post report.md as a sticky comment

- if: steps.weft.outputs.status == 'suspended'
  run: echo "awaiting ${{ steps.weft.outputs.pendingQuestion }}"

# and the resume half
on:
  issue_comment:
    types: [created]
jobs:
  resume:
    if: startsWith(github.event.comment.body, '@weft ')
    steps:
      - uses: techery/weft-resume-action@v1
        with: { run-id: ${{ ... }}, comment: ${{ github.event.comment.body }} }

# locally, the same thing
$ weft run review --budget '500k,$5' --read-only --json > result.json
$ echo $?   # 0 done · 1 failed · 2 suspended · 3 budget
priorArt: gh-aw compiles Markdown+YAML into ordinary GitHub Actions and enforces that the agent job is read-only while writes go through schema-validated safe outputs applied by a separately permissioned job — the strongest security architecture in the CI-agent group. Claude Code Action posts a live-updating checklist comment in the PR thread. Braintrust's GitHub Action runs evals and comments score diffs on every PR. Trigger.dev and Temporal both expose CLI verbs designed for exactly this kind of scripting.
risks: Artifact-based state handoff between jobs is real but clunky — artifacts expire, and a run whose journal is only in a 90-day artifact is not durable in any meaningful sense; the honest framing is that CI weft needs either a shared store (S3/Postgres JournalStore) or short-lived gates. The `--read-only` integrate refusal needs a real mechanism, not a flag the workflow can ignore: the cleanest version is a config-level policy the workflow cannot override, which weft currently has no concept of. Posting reports to PRs means step outputs (journaled verbatim, including exec stdout) reach a possibly-public surface.
fitsArchitecture: Depends on the `--json` and exit-code work; consumes the bridge for the comment half. A new repo for the action itself, plus in-tree: `packages/cli` gains `--read-only` and the documented exit codes, `packages/host/src/config.ts` gains a `policy` section for constraints a workflow cannot relax, and `packages/core` gains the enforcement point in `ctx.integrate`. A `.github/workflows/` example in-tree doubles as the smoke test.

title: Workflow packages: `weft add`, npm distribution, and a lockfile
problem: The registry is a directory of `*.ts` files (`packages/gate/src/registry.ts`) keyed by basename or `meta.name`, cached by bundle hash. That is a good local design and a dead end for sharing: there is no way to install someone else's workflow, no versioning, no dependency story, and `weft new` produces a blank-ish two-phase template that is the only starting point anyone gets. Meanwhile the determinism gate's `allowBare` already understands that some imports are legitimate and `bundleWorkflow` already inlines everything else — so distribution is closer than it looks. Adoption of a workflow engine is gated on whether a team can get value before writing TypeScript, and weft's answer today is "write TypeScript."
proposal: Make a workflow package an ordinary npm package exporting one or more `WorkflowDefinition`s plus a `weft.workflows` field in its manifest. `weft add @acme/weft-review` installs it, resolves the exported workflows, and writes `.weft/workflows.lock.json` recording each workflow's name, package version, and — crucially — its bundle hash, which is the same hash `run.created` stamps as `defHash`, so a resume can tell whether the workflow it is resuming has been upgraded underneath it. The registry gains a second source: after scanning `workflows.dir` it resolves lockfile entries, bundling each package's entry with the merged allowBare. `weft add --eject <name>` copies a package workflow into `workflows.dir` as editable source, which is the shadcn model and the right escape hatch for something you will inevitably want to modify. Ship a first-party `@techery/weft-workflows` bundle with the four workflows everyone writes anyway: PR review, dependency-bump-and-verify, test-flake triage, and codemod-across-files — each gate-clean, each with a conformance golden file, each usable via `weft run review --pr 412` with no authoring at all.
priorArt: Claude Code's plugin/marketplace model bundles agents, skills, hooks, workflows and commands as installable units. goose's Recipe Cookbook distributes recipes as shareable YAML. iii's `iii worker add` makes extending the runtime an operational command against a registry. shadcn/ui's copy-into-your-repo model is the prior art for `--eject`. Claude Code Action's curated solution templates (PR review, issue triage, doc sync) are the cheapest adoption lever any of these tools has.
risks: Installing a third-party workflow means running third-party code — the determinism gate constrains what it can do (no network, no process.env, no bare imports outside the allowlist) but the AGENTS the workflow dispatches are unconstrained, and a hostile workflow's prompt is a prompt-injection vector into your repo. Package workflows need the same `allowBare` merge the local registry does, and a package that requests a broad allowlist is a red flag the install should surface. Lockfile bundle hashes will churn on every transitive dependency change, which is correct and will be annoying. Bundling a package's workflow through esbuild with its dependencies inlined can produce very large bundles.
fitsArchitecture: `packages/gate/src/registry.ts` gains a second candidate source and a lockfile reader; the hash-keyed cache and tolerantLoad behaviour carry over unchanged. `packages/host/src/weft.ts` passes the lockfile path alongside `workflows.dir`. `packages/cli` gains `weft add`/`weft remove`. A new in-repo `packages/workflows` holds the first-party bundle, which also gives the two example workflows in `.weft/workflows/` a real home and gives CI something meatier than a smoke test.

title: Claude Code integration kit: make weft the thing Claude Code reaches for
problem: weft's authoring model is plain TypeScript, which is maximally flexible and therefore maximally blank-page — and the agent most likely to write a weft workflow is Claude Code, which knows nothing about weft. Meanwhile weft's MCP server exists but is one of many, and `weft_types` returns the SDK source as a text blob rather than as anything discoverable. And a weft write step hands an agent a fresh worktree stripped of `AGENTS.md`, the repository-conventions file that Codex, Claude Code, Copilot, Cursor, Aider and 60,000+ repos already use and that is now under Linux Foundation governance — free interop weft is declining.
proposal: Three pieces. (1) `weft init --claude` writes `.claude/skills/weft/SKILL.md` (when and how to author a weft workflow, the ctx surface, the determinism rules with their fix-its, the gate/budget/integrate idioms) plus a `.mcp.json` entry pointing at `weft-mcp` — so a Claude Code session in the repo can author, run, and answer weft workflows without a human pasting docs. (2) Expose `weft_types` as MCP *resources* rather than a tool, one per SDK file, so the host can pull them into context on demand; and add a `weft_check` tool wrapping the determinism gate so the model gets `file:line:col rule message` + `fix:` feedback and can self-correct before ever running anything. That closes the loop: the model writes, the gate rejects with an actionable fix-it, the model repairs — the same repair pattern weft already applies to step outputs, applied to workflow authoring. (3) `AgentRequest` gains a `context?: { agentsMd?: string }` and the engine reads the nearest `AGENTS.md` chain (nearest-wins, like the convention specifies) from the integration tree, writes it into each worktree, and journals which files were in scope so a replay is faithful when the file changes. (4) Ship `weft mcp --cwd <dir> --mock` argv parsing — today `packages/mcp/src/bin.ts` takes no arguments and always uses `process.cwd()` with real providers, so it can only be pointed at a repo by the spawn cwd.

$ weft init --claude
  wrote .claude/skills/weft/SKILL.md
  wrote .mcp.json  (weft → weft-mcp --cwd .)
  wrote AGENTS.md  (stub; weft passes this into every write step)

priorArt: microsandbox and Claude Code both ship MCP servers exposing their own primitives so external agents can drive them. Windmill generates LLM tool JSON Schemas automatically from typed function signatures so tool definitions never drift from implementations. PocketFlow's explicit design constraint is that the entire framework fits in a coding agent's context window, and its authors treat that as the reason an LLM can write correct PocketFlow code. AGENTS.md is honoured by Codex, Claude Code, Copilot, Jules, goose, Cursor and Aider — declining it is the only real choice weft is making here.
risks: A skill file is documentation that rots the moment the SDK changes; it should be generated from the same source `weft_types` reads, not hand-maintained. Passing AGENTS.md into a worktree means untrusted repository prose reaches the agent's prompt — for a public repo that is a prompt-injection surface, and the content must be journaled (so a replay is faithful) and clearly delimited in the prompt. `weft_check` exposed over MCP lets a model bundle arbitrary source through esbuild, which is a compile-bomb surface that needs a size and time cap.
fitsArchitecture: `packages/cli/src/commands/new.ts` grows an `init --claude` sibling. `packages/mcp` changes most: `src/tools.ts` gains `weft_check`, `src/typings.ts` becomes a resource provider, `src/bin.ts` gains argv parsing for `--cwd`/`--mock`. `packages/core/src/provider.ts` `AgentRequest` gains the optional context field and `packages/core/src/ctx.ts` reads the AGENTS.md chain when seeding a worktree (it already builds the worktree at ctx.ts:406-423). `packages/provider-claude` and `-codex` pass it through in their prompt assembly.

title: Redaction pass over everything that leaves the journal
problem: Secret redaction covers only env maps and fetch header names/values passed as SecretHandles (ctx.ts:109-158). Step outputs are journaled verbatim: exec/bash stdout+stderr, fetch response bodies and headers, agent prompts, and `ctx.env.get`'s actual value all land in `journal.jsonl` unredacted. That is defensible while the journal never leaves the machine — and every idea in this brief (notifications, bridges to public PRs, OTel export, artifact upload in CI, sharing a run for debugging) makes it leave the machine. A redaction story is a prerequisite for the product surface, not a follow-up to it.
proposal: A single `redact(value, policy)` pass in core with three consumers and one authoring primitive. (1) Detectors: a default set (AWS keys, GitHub PATs, private key blocks, JWTs, high-entropy strings adjacent to `token`/`secret`/`key`, plus every literal value in `process.env` that came from a declared `ctx.secret` name) and a config-extensible pattern list. (2) An authoring primitive `ctx.redacted(value)` that marks a value so it is journaled as `<redacted:sha256[0:8]>` — the hash makes it comparable across replays without disclosing it, which matters because the journal is also a replay authority. (3) Apply at the boundary, not at write: the journal stays verbatim (it is the local source of truth and redacting it would break replay), and the pass runs on every export path — `weft otel export`, notify payloads, bridge comments, CI artifact upload, `weft cat`, and the daemon's blob routes. Add a `.weft/config.json` `redaction: { mode: "strict" | "warn" | "off", patterns: [...] }` where strict refuses to export anything containing a detector hit rather than silently masking it. Add a `weft scan <run>` verb that reports what a given run would leak, so the answer is knowable before anything is shared.
priorArt: OpenInference specifies attribute masking/privacy controls applied at instrumentation time, and the OTel GenAI conventions make instrumentation-level filtering and truncation of captured message content an explicit expectation. Google ADK's `temp:` state key prefix is a sanctioned never-persisted escape hatch — the authoring-primitive half of this. Microsoft Agent Framework treats checkpoint storage as an explicit trust boundary with a documented threat model and a deserialization allowlist, which is the framing weft's README should adopt.
risks: Detector-based redaction is a heuristic and will both miss things and false-positive on legitimate content (a diff that adds a test fixture with a fake key). Strict mode blocking export on a false positive is annoying and is still the right default for anything leaving the machine. `ctx.redacted` changes a value's journaled representation, so it must not be usable on anything the replay path needs to reproduce — the hash placeholder makes matching work but the value itself is gone on replay, which is the same trade `ctx.secret` already makes and must be documented identically. Scanning large journals with many regexes is slow enough to need caching.
fitsArchitecture: New module `packages/core/src/redact.ts` next to the existing `jsonUnsafeAt` walker in jsonschema.ts, which already does exactly this shape of traversal and can be generalized. `ctx.redacted` is one addition to `packages/sdk/src/types.ts` and `packages/core/src/ctx.ts`. `packages/host/src/config.ts` gains the section. Consumers — notify, bridge, otel, cli export paths, daemon blob routes — all call the same function, which is the point: one policy, many boundaries.

title: `isolation: "sandbox"` — a real boundary under the worktree
problem: The README is honest that node:vm is a determinism fence and not a security boundary, but the gap is wider than that: the AGENT's process is not sandboxed at all. Worktree isolation is convention — a write step can `fs.writeFile` anywhere on the machine, and weft learns about it only from provider-self-reported `filesTouched`, with posix-only escape detection (`isAbsolute(p) || p.startsWith("../")`, ctx.ts:631). Codex reports `filesTouched: []` by design, so under Codex there is no witness at all. And `ctx.fetch` allows every host unless `fetchAllow` is explicitly configured — the field is optional and undefined by default (config.ts:52-55), and the hardened per-hop redirect validation is skipped entirely when there is no allow-list and no credential-shaped header. A step that installs dependencies also mutates global caches, opens ports, and writes to $HOME, none of which the worktree discards.
proposal: Add a `SandboxBackend` seam next to the existing worktree machinery, selected per step by `isolation: "sandbox"` or configured as the default for write steps. Backend one, and the one to build first: Anthropic's `sandbox-runtime` shape — bubblewrap on Linux, Seatbelt on macOS, with reads deny-then-allow, writes ALLOW-ONLY scoped to the worktree path (which makes the declared `write.paths` scope enforced rather than checked after the fact), and network deny-all behind a host proxy with a per-step domain allowlist. This is a process-tree wrapper: no container, no VM, no daemon, so it fits weft's local-first posture and is installable wherever weft already runs. Backend two: `microsandbox` (libkrun microVMs as child processes, <100ms boot, TS SDK) for untrusted repos, and `container-use`/Docker for teams already there. Every denial is journaled as a `sandbox.denied` event, which turns the boundary into a diagnostic surface — you learn exactly which command the agent tried to run outside its scope, which today you learn never. Separately and independently: flip `fetchAllow` to default-deny with an explicit `["*"]` opt-out, because a default that silently permits arbitrary egress from a step running model-generated code is the wrong default regardless of sandboxing.
priorArt: Anthropic's sandbox-runtime is exactly this shape — bubblewrap/Seatbelt/WFP process-tree scoping with writes allow-only and network deny-all behind a proxy domain allowlist — and it exists precisely so Claude Code can drop approval prompts for actions whose blast radius is provably contained. OpenAI Codex CLI pins sandbox_mode (read-only/workspace-write/danger-full-access) via Seatbelt/Landlock/seccomp and protects .git even in writable modes, treating approval_policy as an orthogonal axis to capability. container-use gives each agent a container so installs and daemons are discarded with the step. microsandbox runs libkrun microVMs as ordinary child processes with a TypeScript SDK. gVisor's "what it isn't" section is the model for the threat-model docs this needs.
risks: Platform coverage is the whole problem: bubblewrap needs Linux, Seatbelt is deprecated-ish Apple surface, and CI runners frequently lack the virtualization or namespace support these need — so the backend must degrade to today's behaviour with a loud, journaled "sandbox unavailable" rather than silently pretending. Over-tight write allowlists break builds in confusing ways, which is why the denial journaling matters more than the enforcement. Flipping fetchAllow to default-deny is a breaking change for anyone relying on the current default and needs a major-version boundary plus a migration note. And this makes the strict/warn asymmetry between Claude (live canUseTool gating) and Codex (nothing) finally symmetric — which is arguably the strongest argument for building it, since `write: { mode: "strict" }` currently means two materially different things depending on which provider a step routed to, behind one advertised interface.
fitsArchitecture: `packages/isolation` gains `src/sandbox.ts` and one backend implementation, sitting alongside the existing worktree.ts and patch.ts — the package boundary is already right. `packages/core/src/ctx.ts` selects the backend where it currently creates the worktree (ctx.ts:406-423) and wraps the provider dispatch. `packages/core/src/events.ts` gains `sandbox.denied`. `packages/sdk/src/types.ts` gains the `sandbox` option on AgentOptions. `packages/host/src/config.ts` gains the `isolation` section and changes the `fetchAllow` default. Provider adapters are untouched — the sandbox wraps the process they spawn, which is exactly why it fixes the Claude/Codex asymmetry without per-adapter work.
